wa_alpine_lookout_round_mountain_trail.name: Round Mountain Trail #1529 to Nason Ridge and the lookout spur
wa_alpine_lookout_round_mountain_trail.notes: From the highway just past the rest area, turn north onto the unsigned Butcher Creek Road (Forest Road 6910) — the turn is on a curve with fast traffic, so watch for it — and follow good gravel a few miles before turning onto the short spur that ends at the Round Mountain Trailhead. Round Mountain Trail #1529 climbs steeply for about a mile and a half through forest and an older burn to its junction with Nason Ridge Trail #1583. Turn left and west and follow the ridge trail, which undulates along the crest for a few miles to the lookout spur.
wa_alpine_lookout_round_mountain_trail.season: Roughly July through October once the ridge melts out; the lookout is one of the few in the range still staffed.
hazards: The turn off the highway is on a blind curve with fast traffic
The ridge trail narrows to a knife edge with steep rock-filled gullies dropping away on both sides
The crest is exposed to weather with no shelter along it
The lower trail climbs steeply through burn with little shade or water
wa_alpine_lookout_round_mountain_trail.baseFinding: A '9' nailed to a tree is the marker, and the knife edge is the confirmation. Walking west along Nason Ridge Trail #1583, the crest pinches down to a ten-foot-wide knife edge with steep, rock-filled gullies falling away to the highway on the south and into the river drainage on the north — that narrowing is Ninemile Saddle, and a sign carrying the numeral 9 is fixed to a tree there. It is the only labelled feature on this stretch of ridge. A few hundred yards past the saddle the trail forks: the Nason Ridge trail drops left toward Merritt Lake, and the lookout trail stays right and climbs the last traverse to the staffed lookout on the summit. The negative marker is simple: if you are losing height off the crest toward Merritt Lake and no building has come into view, you took the left fork and should go back to the junction just past the narrow section with the numbered tree.

wa_alpine_lookout_round_mountain_trail.name: Merritt Lake trail from the west
wa_alpine_lookout_round_mountain_trail.notes: A longer way in reaches the same ridge trail from the west via the Merritt Lake trail. It is used mainly for through-hikes or when the Round Mountain side is inaccessible.

wa_buckner_mountain_north_face.name: Boston Basin, Sharkfin Col rappel, and south across the Boston Glacier to the schrund
wa_buckner_mountain_north_face.notes:
Start from the Boston Basin trailhead near 3,200 ft, about 21.7 miles up Cascade River Road — a different and shorter drive than the Cascade Pass trailhead used for the southwest route. The climbers' path follows an old overgrown mining road about a mile to a former mine site, then a steep boot path through old growth with roughly four creek crossings, emerging above treeline near 5,300 ft into Boston Basin: about 2.5 miles and 3,100 ft, typically three to four hours. Camp low at about 5,300 ft or high at 6,300-6,400 ft; NPS permit required and camping restricted to the established sites.

From high camp, follow the Quien Sabe Glacier route roped, and climb toward Sharkfin Col rather than taking the loose class 3-4 scramble around Boston Peak. Many parties gain the ridge just east of the col, where a natural or fixed sling anchor is used for a short rappel — or, in leaner conditions, a steep no-fall-zone downclimb on crumbly mixed rock — onto the Boston Glacier. Multiple trip reports flag this as the technical crux of the approach, sometimes harder than the climbing above.

Once on the Boston Glacier, rope up and traverse south toward the base of Buckner's north face, zig-zagging around the schrund and large crevasses near the toe, with some rock scrambling to bypass the gap. Many parties bivy on the glacier itself around 7,800 ft to shorten summit day.
wa_buckner_mountain_north_face.season: Late May through early July for the best face conditions
hazards: A short rappel or a steep no-fall-zone downclimb off Sharkfin Col on crumbly mixed rock — the crux of the approach, and it has to be reversed
A viciously crevassed upper Boston Glacier with cracks scattered randomly across the ice
A bergschrund at the toe of the face that can run its full width, needing rock scrambling to bypass
Wind-scoured ice on some ascents and moderate powder on others — the face's character changes completely with conditions
Cornices on the summit ridge, and rockfall as the day warms
wa_buckner_mountain_north_face.baseFinding:
The base is the bergschrund at the toe of the face, on the Boston Glacier, and the position test is directional: from the col you traverse south across the glacier. If you turned north you are heading for Forbidden's north side.

The entry move is a zig-zag and it is the positive test: work climber's left of the bergschrund, then back right into the centre of the lower face, and then straight up. Left, right, up. A party that crossed the schrund directly and started climbing where it stood has not found the line the face is climbed on.

What you are climbing confirms it: about 1,300 ft of 40-50 degree snow and ice, continuous, with no rock pitches. If you are on rock below the summit ridge, you have drifted off the face.

The finish is the other countable point, and getting it wrong costs time at the worst moment: continue straight up until upper rock cliffs force a rising traverse to the left. Then, within about 200 ft of the summit, go left around a craggy rock outcrop at the end of those cliffs, and only then back right to the top. Both moves are left. A party that goes right at the cliff band has misread the finish.

And the approach itself is the strongest negative test against this peak's other route: the Southwest Face is reached over Cascade Pass, Sahale Arm and Horseshoe Basin, on the opposite side of the mountain, and the two share no ground until the summit ridge. If you walked past an old mine in a basin at 7,000 ft, you are on the southwest route.

wa_buckner_mountain_north_face.name: Over Sahale and the Boston-Sahale col from Sahale Glacier Camp
wa_buckner_mountain_north_face.notes: A second way in reaches the same glacier over Sahale and the Boston-Sahale col from Sahale Glacier Camp.

wa_cosho_peak_scramble.name: Cosho Camp to the 7,830 ft saddle and the north snowfield
wa_cosho_peak_scramble.notes: From Cosho Camp continue west down the Fisher Creek Trail about a mile and leave it at one of the gullies due south of the Cosho-Kimtah saddle, starting around 3,800 ft. The climb up is the crux of the day: sustained bushwhacking through trees and brush for the first thousand feet, then loose, tedious scree and steep grass with occasional solid rock, roughly 4,000 ft of gain to the saddle at about 7,830 ft.
hazards: Four thousand feet of loose, brushy off-trail gain with no water above the creek
Firm snow on the north side of the saddle — carry an ice axe
Remote and rarely visited; navigating back to the correct gully in poor visibility is the real danger
The wrong gully on the way down leads into brush
wa_cosho_peak_scramble.baseFinding: At the saddle, cross to the north side and climb snow until it runs out. From the 7,830 ft saddle the route does not follow the crest: step over onto the snowfield on the north side and climb moderate snow northwest to roughly 8,100 ft. Where the snow ends is the base of the climbing — a couple of hundred feet of third-class rock on the upper east face, reported mostly solid, with cairns marking the stretches where the ground is ambiguous, finishing at the summit. That snow-to-rock transition at about 8,100 ft is the test. If you are still on talus and scree on the south side of the saddle with no snowfield below you, you have not crossed over. If you are working up a broad crest with no snow anywhere, you are on the wrong saddle: the correct one lies due north of the point at which you left the Fisher Creek Trail, between Cosho and Kimtah.

wa_cosho_peak_scramble.name: From Kimtah, down the south gully and the connecting traverse
wa_cosho_peak_scramble.notes: This way is used by parties combining Cosho with Kimtah: they descend Kimtah's south gully and follow cairns down the connecting traverse to the same saddle.

wa_diamond_in_the_rough.name: Bedal Creek to the Southwest Face basin
wa_diamond_in_the_rough.notes:
Bedal Creek is the preferred trailhead for this side of the peak because it avoids the river fords. FR 4096 off the Mountain Loop Highway, about 18.25 miles south of Darrington and roughly a mile south of Bedal Campground; the spur is rough and narrow. Trailhead about 2,790 ft.

Bedal Creek Trail #705 through old growth and along the creek's steep banks until the tread ends at a large washout, roughly one and a half to two and a half miles in. Scramble the washout to a cairned exit onto the climbers' path, which leaves left near 48.0560, -121.3631 around 3,500 ft under pink flagging and switchbacks steeply up to about 4,900 ft. Talus and meadow then lead to the 5,300 ft Bedal-Sloan saddle — last reliable water before the wall.

This is a full day of walking before a long rock route.
hazards: Large washout with loose boulders and blowdown at the end of the maintained trail
Brush and real route-finding in the forest band
North Fork Sauk ford if approaching from FR 49
Long committing day — the base alone is most of a full day's walking
wa_diamond_in_the_rough.baseFinding: From the saddle, cross the low connecting ridge into the Southwest Face basin and its meadows rather than continuing onto the glacier. The base of the wall is gained from meadow and talus, dry-shod. Stepping onto glacier ice means you are on the Corkscrew approach, not this one.

wa_diamond_in_the_rough.name: Cougar Creek and the North Fork Sauk from FR 49
wa_diamond_in_the_rough.notes: This way starts from FR 49 and reaches the same basin from the north. It requires fording the North Fork Sauk plus a cold Cougar Creek crossing, slide alder and devil's club.

wa_dumbell_mountain_west.name: Phelps Creek Trail #1511 to Spider Meadow and upper Phelps Basin
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.notes:
From the Phelps Creek Trailhead at about 3,500 ft at the end of FR-6211, follow Phelps Creek Trail #1511 north up the east side of the creek. It climbs gently — roughly 1,900 ft over five or six miles — through old and second growth, with several small side streams giving reliable water the whole way. After a heavy avalanche winter the tread threads graveyards of downed timber pushed across it from the slopes to the west.

Spider Meadow near 5,150-5,400 ft is the last easy, reliable water. Walk the length of the meadow to its head, where the trail forks. The fork is unsigned: the left branch carries on toward Spider Gap and Larch Knob, and the Dumbell path is the right-hand one, an old climbers' trail into lower Phelps Basin. Most parties camp in the basin around 5,700 to 6,000 ft.

Note that FR-6200 has been closed beyond Atkinson Flat under a storm-damage order, which blocks the drive to this trailhead entirely.
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.season: Late Jul-Sep. Before that the approach gully and the upper basin are full snow, wanting an axe and often crampons; snow returns to the upper mountain by late September
hazards: Several parallel gullies and ledge systems on the south face that look identical and do not all go — the documented way to get cliffed out here
A reported truck-sized snow block perched on a slab near 8,000 ft in the direct south-face gully
Loose rock and rubble in the gully and on the summit ledges, with parties above you
Lookalike notches and false summits near the top
FR-6200 closed beyond Atkinson Flat under a storm-damage order, which blocks the standard drive entirely
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.baseFinding:
The approach to the climbing is a creek, and it is the only way through an otherwise cliffy face. From camp in upper Phelps Basin, leave the last of the boot path and head east-north-east beside a tumbling side creek. That creek cuts the one weakness in the cliffs above the basin; the broad talus-and-scree gully on Dumbell's south side follows it. If you are working up an open face with no water beside you, you are not in the breach.

The first arrival is a notch on the south-east shoulder, around 7,900 ft, reached by climbing that gully out of the basin directly south of the summit. Grass and heather give way to talus and — through about mid-August — moderate snow.

Then comes the measurement that decides the day, and it is counted in yards rather than looked for: from the notch, go 100 to 200 yards left — west — and take the gully there. Not the gully at the notch. Aim for the right-hand side of the south face, where the easiest gully system starts. Several parallel gullies and ledge lines look alike here and they do not all go: the wrong one cliffs you out below the summit ridge.

What confirms you chose right: a little scrambling above that gully gains a system of ledges which then zig-zags up onto the West Ridge. Ledges that zig-zag rather than a continuous line, and a ridge crest at the top of them, is the confirmation. A gully that runs out against steeper rock with no ledge system is the wrong one — go back down and try further west.

The summit warning is real and it is about lookalikes: from the west ridge a few hundred feet of easy but exposed Class 3 leads to the top, and similar-looking notches and false summits near the top have sent parties astray. Keep track of which top you are on rather than assuming the first one is it.

One object to know about: a party has reported an unstable, truck-sized snow block perched on a slab near 8,000 ft in the direct south-face gully. Treat the direct line under it as loaded ground rather than a shortcut.

wa_dumbell_mountain_west.name: Spider Gap from Railroad Creek and Lyman Lake (Holden Village)
wa_dumbell_mountain_west.notes: A longer alternate reaches the same basin from the east over Spider Gap from Railroad Creek and Lyman Lake out of Holden Village. It is used by parties already doing that loop, not as a way in.

wa_fortress_mountain_east_ridge.name: Trinity and the Chiwawa River Trail to the Chiwawa-Fortress col
wa_fortress_mountain_east_ridge.notes:
From Trinity Trailhead near 2,800 ft at the end of FR-6200, follow the Buck Creek and Chiwawa River trails up-valley, staying left at the Red Mountain junction near 5 mi and fording the Chiwawa River. Beyond the ford leave the trail and climb open forest to a basin near 5,500 ft and a bench near 6,300 ft, then traverse diagonally up toward Chiwawa Mountain's east ridge, descending to the roughly 7,200 ft col between Chiwawa and Fortress. Some parties go over Chiwawa's summit first instead. Others approach by way of the Red Mountain Trail and Chiwawa Basin — the same basin the Chiwawa Mountain route uses, which puts you on the col from below rather than from along the ridge.

The col is a common high camp and this route is very often combined with Chiwawa Mountain from it, which is the practical reason to camp there rather than lower.

Rock quality is notably better on the East Ridge itself than in the gully that gains it or on Fortress's south-west face — the opposite of what most parties expect.

Storm damage has closed FR-6200 to vehicles beyond Atkinson Flat, adding roughly seven miles of road-walking each way; check its status with the Wenatchee River Ranger District before you go.
wa_fortress_mountain_east_ridge.season: Jun-Oct. Crampons and an axe are commonly used on the snow slopes crossing to the col even in late summer
hazards: Loose rock in the gully gaining the East Ridge from the col — the worst ground on the route, and reversed on the way down
An exposed, normally unroped fourth-class step on the final summit pitch
Cold thigh- to knee-deep fords of the Chiwawa River drainage on the approach
Steep firm snow crossing to the col, wanting crampons and an axe even late in the season
About seven extra miles of road-walking each way while FR-6200 is closed beyond Atkinson Flat
wa_fortress_mountain_east_ridge.baseFinding:
The col is the camp and the gully is the route, and they are not the same place. From the roughly 7,200 ft Chiwawa-Fortress col, the East Ridge is gained by a loose class 3-4 gully. Standing on the col is not standing at the base; you still have a gully to find and climb before the ridge starts.

The rock itself is the confirmation, and it works backwards from what you would guess: the gully is the loose ground and the ridge above it is the solid ground. So the test that you have topped out of the correct gully onto the correct crest is that the rock gets better. If you have gained a crest and it is still rubble, you are on a subsidiary rib rather than the East Ridge.

The discriminator against the other route on this mountain: the south-west face is reached from an entirely different valley — Buck Creek Trail and Pass No Pass at about 6,400 ft — and never comes near this col. If your approach involved a way-trail and a pass rather than a cross-country traverse off the Chiwawa River Trail, you are on the other side of the peak.

The finish is one move and it is unprotected in practice: an exposed fourth-class step just below the summit, normally climbed unroped. That step is the route's crux and its arrival marker — reaching it means the ridge is behind you.

Coming back down, the head of the gully is the thing to find, and it is easier to walk past from above than from below. Follow the crest back until the ground drops away toward the col, and descend carefully; the gully is the loosest part of the day in both directions.

If you continue to Chiwawa Mountain from the col — which many parties do — note that its route works up the south-west side on slabs and talus from that same col, so the two climbs share a base and diverge immediately.

wa_fortress_mountain_east_ridge.name: Red Mountain Trail into Chiwawa Basin, then up to the Chiwawa-Fortress col
wa_fortress_mountain_east_ridge.notes: Start at Trinity as for the main way, but at the fork where the valley trail splits, take the right branch onto the Red Mountain Trail instead of carrying on toward the river ford. About 3.7 miles up the Red Mountain Trail a smaller, less obvious path turns off downhill to the left; it drops a few hundred feet into the Chiwawa Basin meadows and fades out near the headwaters of the river. From the meadows climb toward the col between Chiwawa Mountain and Fortress at about 7,200 ft, which has good camping, and pick up the East Ridge from there.

wa_mount_angeles_standard.name: Klahhane Ridge climbers' trail from Hurricane Ridge
wa_mount_angeles_standard.notes: Paved path off the east end of the visitor centre lot, then open subalpine ridge for about two and a half miles to an unsigned split. A shorter, steeper start climbs from the Switchback Trail on the road below and joins higher up. Nothing dependable to drink past the visitor centre — carry it all.
hazards: Fractured, rotten rock on the summit block with holds that break
Rockfall funnelling down the crux gully onto anyone below
Rotten snow choking the summit notch into July and August
Exposed Class 3 moves with a fall of well over a hundred feet
Fast-building afternoon storms on a fully exposed ridge
Nothing dependable to drink past the visitor centre
wa_mount_angeles_standard.baseFinding: The climbers' path leaves the maintained Klahhane Ridge Trail at an unsigned fork roughly 2.3 miles out: bear left and uphill to the north, where the maintained tread carries on right along the ridge toward Victor Pass and Lake Angeles. From the fork the primitive path climbs rocky meadow on the peak's west side and does about eight hundred of the day's feet in a little over half a mile, topping out near 6,000 ft in a scree bowl beneath the summit block. The identification that matters here is which notch, and it catches people every season: do not scramble the first notch you reach. The boot path keeps traversing higher and the gully that goes is further along, directly beneath the true summit. Stay on the worn tread climber's-left of the open scree fan rather than going straight up the fan itself, which is the rockfall funnel. You are at the base when the meadow ends and you are standing on dirty, fractured ledges with a roughly forty-foot exposed step above you. If the ground has levelled off or you are back on maintained tread heading toward Lake Angeles, you have overshot.

wa_mount_angeles_standard.name: Switchback Trail up to Klahhane Ridge

bivy.name: Heart o' the Hills campground
bivy.notes: This is the staging base for Mount Angeles and it is a staging base only — it is a few miles up the Hurricane Ridge road from Port Angeles, and no part of the climb passes through it. The scramble itself starts from a pull-out around mile 15 on that road, where the Switchback trail gains about 700 ft in six-tenths of a mile to its junction with the trail from Hurricane Ridge, then about half a mile west along that trail and a spur onto the unmaintained final ridge — exposed walking and class 3 on loose fractured rock to the 6,454 ft summit. It is a day trip for a fit party, so this camp exists for the group that starts late, gets weathered off, or wants to be at the trailhead at first light. Read the road before you count on it: in winter the Hurricane Ridge road is plowed and open only Friday through Sunday plus a few holiday dates, with uphill traffic released from mid-morning, and it closes without notice in bad weather. Recent seasons have also brought midweek closures for utility work in the weeks after Memorial Day, so check the current schedule rather than assuming summer means open. Because there are no reservations, arrive early on a summer weekend.
bivy.water: Drinking water on tap, flush toilets and rubbish collection through the season
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit — frontcountry campground, nightly fee paid on site, park entrance fee applies. Fires permitted in the provided rings unless a seasonal ban is in force, which happens most late summers on this peninsula.
bivy.capacity: Around 105 single-family sites in old growth, taking tents and rigs up to about 24 ft with a few longer; first-come, first-served with no reservations

wa_mount_angeles_standard.notes: A steep, short trail from the Hurricane Ridge Road up to the Klahhane Ridge trail, then the same climbers' path to the summit.
hazards: Steep, short trail from the road up to the Klahhane Ridge trail
Fractured, rotten rock on the summit block with holds that break

Fast-building afternoon storms on a fully exposed ridge

wa_mount_angeles_standard.notes: The long way from low on the Hurricane Ridge Road: the Heather Park trail climbs around the west side of the peak to join the climbers' path.
hazards: Long approach on the Heather Park trail from Heart O' the Hills, around the west side of the peak
Fractured, rotten rock on the summit block with holds that break

wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.name: Park Creek Pass and the heather traverse to the Fremont saddle and the hogsback
camps: Meadows north of Park Creek Pass
Valley camps on the walk in
wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.notes:
The standard start is the Colonial Creek Campground trailhead on SR-20 near milepost 130, about 1,060-1,200 ft, and the Thunder Creek trail south for roughly 16-18 miles to the Thunder Basin camp area around 6,000 ft and on to Park Creek Pass.

From Park Creek Pass leave the maintained trail and traverse gradually northward around a broad ridge through open heather and high alpine terrain, roughly a mile and a half to two miles, crossing a rib around 7,600 ft and a steep gully through cliff bands around 7,350 ft that can hold snow or ice. That brings you to the Fremont Glacier saddle around 8,000-8,250 ft, where rock-outcrop bivy sites with nearby running water make the standard high camp.

From camp it is about three and a half hours to the summit.
hazards: Crevasses on the Fremont Glacier, generally small but present
Bergschrund opens below the summit ridge late season as the snow finger melts, plus a moat at the crest
Exposed, often unroped Class 3-4 scrambling on the summit ridge
Steep gully through cliff bands near 7,350 ft can hold snow or ice
Long unmaintained cross-country route-finding above the moraine camp
Hazardous footlog crossings over Thunder Creek at night or high water; no fixed anchors for rappels
wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.baseFinding:
The base is the Hogsback — the snow spine at the upper edge of the Fremont Glacier, on the peak's south ridge. You reach it by a gentle glacier crossing from the saddle camp, and there is a moat crossing to step from the snow onto the crest, which late in the season may have no bridge left at all. Snow spine plus a gap to step across is the confirmation you are at the start.

Then count three features in order, and the order is the whole route-finding problem: a class 3-4 rock pitch gains a left-slanting ramp — a fault-line weakness in the cliff bands — to the summit ridge; then exposed class 2-3 ledges on the east side of the ridge lead through a U-notch between the summit tower and the south horn; then a final class 3-4 pitch of about 100 ft on good holds and solid rock reaches the tiny summit.

The strongest negative test is the ramp: if you are trying to climb the summit tower directly from the glacier, you have missed it. The ramp is the way through the cliff bands and it slants left. Going straight at the tower puts you on ground the route deliberately avoids.

The U-notch is the second confirmation and it is a shape, not a height: a U-shaped gap between the summit tower and the south horn, reached by traversing ledges on the ridge's east flank. If you never dropped onto the east side, you did not take the ledges.

And know which side of the mountain you are on before you start: this is the southeast/southwest approach, from Park Creek Pass. The Douglas Glacier route comes from Easy Pass and the Douglas Creek alder on the northeast; the Banded Glacier route comes from Fisher Creek and gains the northeast ridge at about 8,800 ft. All three finish on the same summit block and share nothing below it.

wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.name: Stehekin and the Park Creek trail to Park Creek Pass

bivy.name: Moraine camp above the pass
bivy.notes: Roughly 6,350 ft, gained by turning east from the meadows and climbing about 500 ft into the moraine of the glacier remnant. Flat, sandy and better protected than the open meadows, and the usual high camp for the Fremont Glacier. From here the route traverses about two miles north around a broad ridge over heather and rock to reach the glacier near 8,000 ft.
bivy.water: Snowmelt off the glacier remnant beside the moraine
bivy.permit: Inside the park; covered by the same backcountry permit as the rest of the route
bivy.capacity: A sheltered flat big enough for a few tents

bivy.name: Meadows north of Park Creek Pass
bivy.notes: Broad sandy meadows a short way north of Park Creek Pass, which itself sits near 6,100 ft. This is where the long valley walk finally ends and the climbing terrain starts; parties either stop here or push the last 500 ft into the moraine above.
bivy.water: Creeks and snowmelt in the meadows below the pass
bivy.permit: Everything on this route is inside North Cascades National Park, so an overnight needs a park backcountry permit and the itinerary is built night by night from designated camps and cross-country zones
bivy.capacity: Open flat ground rather than built sites; a few parties at a time

bivy.name: Valley camps on the walk in
bivy.notes: The approach is long enough that most parties sleep at least one night in the forest before reaching climbing terrain — Thunder Basin in the upper Thunder Creek drainage from the Colonial Creek side, or Buckner Camp on Park Creek (named for the mountain, not on it) coming in from Stehekin. Park Creek has to be crossed near some of these camps and is worth doing in daylight.
bivy.water: Thunder Creek and Park Creek run beside these camps
bivy.permit: Designated North Cascades camps, reserved by name for specific nights on the backcountry permit; Stehekin-side parties can obtain the permit at the ranger station there
bivy.capacity: Established backcountry sites with a fixed number of parties each

wa_mount_logan_fremont_glacier.notes: From the Park Creek Trailhead on the Stehekin Valley Road, the Park Creek trail climbs to Park Creek Pass and joins the Thunder Creek line there. It needs the Lake Chelan boat and the Stehekin shuttle to reach the trailhead. The way in starts at the High Bridge guard station near 1,600 ft, follows the Stehekin River trail to the Park Creek trailhead, then takes the Park Creek trail past Buckner Camp, with a creek crossing on a less-than-substantial footlog that is genuinely nerve-wracking in the dark.
hazards: Footlog crossing on Park Creek, hazardous at night or in high water
Steep gully through cliff bands near 7,350 ft above Park Creek Pass can hold snow or ice
Crevasses on the Fremont Glacier, generally small but present
Bergschrund opens below the summit ridge late season, plus a moat at the crest
Exposed, often unroped Class 3-4 scrambling on the summit ridge
Long unmaintained cross-country route-finding above the moraine camp; no fixed anchors for rappels

wa_ne_ridge.name: Upper Cathedral Lake camp, then the grassy south-east slope onto the ridge
camps: Cathedral Pass benches and the tarn slabs
wa_ne_ridge.notes:
Reach Upper Cathedral Lake at about 7,380 ft by any of the long trails — Andrews Creek #504 is the shortest drive, the Cathedral Driveway #510A the shortest walk, Thirtymile via the Chewuch #510 the middle option. All are multi-day and all put you in the same basin.

From the Boundary Trail below the peak, this route does not go into the Cathedral–Monk gully at all. Scramble up the grassy south-east slope directly from the main trail to gain the ridge.
hazards: Loose rock on a long broken ridge
Continuing north along the crest leads toward The Pope and the Canadian border, which is not lawful to cross
Afternoon thunderstorms on the exposed ridge
Very long walk out from a remote basin if anything goes wrong
A no-fall step-across on the walk-off descent
wa_ne_ridge.baseFinding:
You are aiming for the long broken ridge that runs between Cathedral Peak and The Pope, a separate small peak further north along the same crest, sitting right on the Canada–United States border.

That relationship is the base-finding and it is also the warning. The ridge has a peak at each end. If you keep working north along the crest past the point where the ground starts descending away from Cathedral, you are heading for The Pope and, shortly after that, for an international border it is illegal to cross here.

The route itself confirms as you go rather than at a single spot: each pitch has a move or two of old-school 5.3 with scrambling between, so seven pitches of mostly-easy ground with occasional short difficulties is correct here and is not a sign you have wandered onto the walk-up. The real crux announces itself — about 400 feet below the summit you cross a dike, and the two short pitches immediately above that dike are the hardest climbing on the route. A final airy fourth-class scramble finishes it.

Negative marker for the start: if you find yourself entering a deep gully with a detached tower on your right, you have walked to the SE Buttress start. The NE Ridge is gained from open grassy slope off the main trail, with no gully involved.

Descent is the ordinary walk-up route to the west, and a short rappel may be wanted to get off the summit ridge.

wa_ne_ridge.name: Cathedral Driveway trail #510A from Loomis via Toats Coulee

bivy.name: Upper Cathedral Lake basin
bivy.notes: The working climbers' camp for both the Southeast Buttress and Amphitheater's ridges, sitting directly under the peaks with short walks to either. The basin has taken heavy use for decades and the Forest Service has posted revegetation closures on damaged ground here in the past, so treat the shoreline as off limits and camp on rock or bare dirt well back from the water. Check the posted signs on arrival rather than assuming last year's layout still applies — which sites are open has changed between seasons. Nights are cold and exposed at this elevation even in August.
bivy.water: The most dependable water anywhere on this approach — the lake holds through the season and needs no rationing. The one place on the route where you can plan on filling without checking a report first.
bivy.permit: Free self-issue Pasayten Wilderness permit at the trailhead you start from. No quota, no reservation, nothing to arrange in advance. Some trailheads also require a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass to park.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites on slabs and benches back from the water; realistically three or four small parties before it feels crowded, and it does fill on midsummer weekends and during larch season

wa_ne_ridge.notes: From the Cathedral Driveway Trailhead on the Toats Coulee road out of Loomis, the trail drops to join the Chewuch trail and then climbs the valley to the Cathedral Lakes basin. The eastern way in, with less climbing than Andrews Creek.

wa_tenpeak_mountain_southeast.name: White River Trail #1507 and the old sheep path into Thunder Basin
wa_tenpeak_mountain_southeast.notes: From Coles Corner take Hwy 207 toward Lake Wenatchee, then White River Road (FR-6400) to its end at the White River / Indian Creek Trailhead near 2,300 ft. Hike White River Trail #1507 about six miles to the Thunder Creek crossing; there is an established camp right at the crossing. Half a mile past Thunder Creek the maintained trail is left behind for an old, unmaintained sheep path that climbs the west side of the Thunder Creek drainage. This is the hard part of the walk in: avalanche debris, blowdown, and dense slide alder choking the tread below the lower basin. Above the alder it opens into a lower basin near 4,175 ft and then climbs steeply into Thunder Basin, an open basin of granite slabs and small tarns which is the standard high camp and has a direct view of the peak. The flat upper basin is near 5,200 ft; the granite slabs and two small tarns at the top of the basin, near 6,400-6,500 ft, are a higher camp closer to the col.
wa_tenpeak_mountain_southeast.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, while the snow between camp and the col is still continuous enough to walk and the summit rock is dry
hazards: Loose, rotten rock in the summit gully and the broken chimney above it, directly over anyone belaying below
Dense slide alder choking the old sheep path below the lower basin — the slowest half-mile of the approach by a wide margin
Crevasses on the small hanging glaciers crossed on the northern approach variations
Cornices and wind-loaded slopes on the approach ridgelines into early summer
White River Road has a repeated history of flash-flood washouts, so the drive is the first thing to verify
wa_tenpeak_mountain_southeast.baseFinding:
The col east of the summit block is the base, and the thing that confirms it is the wind. Parties who have stood there describe it as an incredibly windy notch below the east face — it is a gap on a ridge, so it funnels, and on a Cascade summit day you will feel it before you can see anything.

Getting there is a single bearing from camp: from Thunder Basin cross talus and snow toward the col that sits east of the summit block, near 8,000 ft. Crampons and an axe are normal for the snow, which stays firm in the morning. You are aiming for the gap beside the summit tower, not for the tower.

The positive test for the start of the climbing: from the col the route takes a loose gully on the left for about 85 ft to a ledge system. Loose first, ledge second. If the first thing above the col is clean solid rock, or if you are moving right rather than left, you are not on it.

The second confirmation is a crack. Above the ledge system the finish is a broken chimney with a good jam crack running up it, and that crack is the one genuinely positive hold-bearing feature on the summit block. Class 4 to easy fifth depending on conditions. If you are on a face with no chimney and no crack, you have drifted off the ledge system.

What it is not: this is a short summit block, not a wall. From the col to the top is roughly two rope lengths. If you have been climbing for hours above the col you are not on this route.

Rack and rock: everything from the col up is loose. Helmet, and space the party out — the gully drops what the leader pulls straight onto whoever is below.

wa_tenpeak_mountain_southeast.name: North Fork Sauk Trail, the PCT and Boulder Pass from the west
wa_tenpeak_mountain_southeast.notes: A far longer way in comes from the west: North Fork Sauk Trail #649 past Mackinaw Shelter to the PCT, then cross-country over Boulder Pass and through the Napeequa to the peak's north and north-east side. Parties who have done it report twenty-plus stream crossings and heavy brush over three days. It is a different trip, not a shortcut.

wa_argonaut_peak_east_ridge.name: Beverly Turnpike TH over Fourth Creek Pass to Porcupine Creek basin
camps: Ingalls Creek valley camps below the Sherpa and Argonaut south sides
Beverly and De Roux campgrounds and the North Fork Teanaway roadside camps
wa_argonaut_peak_east_ridge.notes:
Beverly Turnpike Trailhead at the end of FR-9737-112, around 3,650 ft. At about half a mile bear left onto signed Trail #1391 (Beverly Turnpike / Beverly Creek). Taking the Bean Creek fork instead is the commonly reported error and costs a lot of the day.

At roughly 3.1 miles turn right onto Trail #1226.1 (Fourth Creek) and climb to Fourth Creek Pass at about 3.6 miles and 5,900-6,000 ft, which opens the first real view of Argonaut, Colchuck and Dragontail. Descend the far side to the south bank of Ingalls Creek at about six miles and 4,200-4,250 ft, and ford — wading or a footlog depending on the season. Flat camping at the Fourth Creek / Ingalls Creek confluence.

From there leave the Ingalls Creek Trail and climb north into the Porcupine Creek drainage on Argonaut's south side: gentle heather and slab, open basin travel, working up beside the southeast ridge. Porcupine Creek basin also holds bivy sites.

Be aware this whole Teanaway-side trail network has been under a Forest Service closure order following the 2025 Labor Mountain Fire — confirm current status with the Cle Elum Ranger District before planning on it.

Note this trailhead is outside the Enchantment Permit Area lottery boundary: a free self-issue wilderness permit covers you, even for an overnight.
hazards: Wrong-fork error onto the Bean Creek trail near the start costs much of the day
Ingalls Creek ford is a real obstacle in early season or after rain
Long, remote approach over Fourth Creek Pass; plan a camp or bivy
Teanaway-side trails under a post-fire closure order; confirm status first
Loose rock on the towers and lichen-covered, hard-to-protect blocks on the lower pitches
Route-finding on the crest between the SE spire false summit and the true summit
Afternoon thunderstorms; long tiring exit
wa_argonaut_peak_east_ridge.baseFinding:
The climb follows the crest of the southeast ridge, which rises from the Ingalls Creek side to the southeast spire, the lowest of Argonaut's three summits. The lower pitches are blocky, lichen-covered and awkward, which is the sign you are on the ridge proper.

Low down, the ridge can be crossed at a notch near 6,750 ft between the south slope and Porcupine Basin; that crossing is a way between the two drainages, not a feature of the climb.

Above the southeast spire, two single-rope rappels or one double-rope rappel take you into the notch, and the route continues to the true summit on the west spire.

wa_argonaut_peak_east_ridge.name: Esmeralda over Longs Pass into Ingalls Creek

bivy.name: Ingalls Creek valley camps below the Sherpa and Argonaut south sides
bivy.notes: This is the base for the south side of both Argonaut and Sherpa, and it is what makes those peaks feasible as overnights rather than brutal single pushes. Two ways in. From Esmeralda you climb to Longs Pass at about 6,200 feet and drop roughly 1,400 feet to the valley, then walk east along the trail until you are under your peak; Sherpa's south basin is about a mile down, Argonaut's exit gully perhaps three. From the low trailhead off US 97 you walk in flat but far, upwards of ten miles to reach the same ground, which trades the pass for distance and suits a party with time. A third link comes over Fourth Creek from the Beverly Creek trailhead in the Teanaway and requires fording Ingalls Creek, which is genuinely dangerous in June. The valley is low and sheltered, so it is buggy through midsummer and warm at night, and the brush between the trail and the open slopes above is the real work of the approach. Sites are dispersed rather than built, so pick an existing one instead of clearing new ground. The elevation of the trail changes across the several miles covered here, so no single figure is given.
bivy.water: Ingalls Creek runs strongly all season and side streams come in from the north wall; the only dry stretch is the climb over Longs Pass, which carries no water at all in either direction
bivy.permit: Alpine Lakes Wilderness under the Cle Elum Ranger District, entirely outside the Enchantment Permit Area. A free self-issued wilderness permit from the trailhead box covers day and overnight use, there is no lottery, no quota and no reservation. A Northwest Forest Pass or day fee is needed to park at Esmeralda; the low Ingalls Creek trailhead off US 97 has its own parking requirement. Campfires are restricted seasonally and are a poor idea in any case; the valley is dry and forested. Camp at least 200 feet from the creek.
bivy.capacity: Numerous flat, well-used sites strung along several miles of valley floor and its side creeks; there is no quota and no realistic crowding, so a party can nearly always find its own ground

bivy.name: Beverly and De Roux campgrounds and the North Fork Teanaway roadside camps
bivy.notes: This is what most parties on Ingalls Peak actually use, because all three Ingalls summits are comfortably a long day from the car and there is no reason to carry a camp. Sleeping on the road puts you at the Esmeralda trailhead in minutes rather than driving up from Cle Elum in the dark. The Ingalls group sits entirely outside the Enchantment Permit Area, in the Cle Elum Ranger District, so the whole permit problem that dominates the Icicle Creek side simply does not exist here: a free self-issued slip at the trailhead, a parking pass, and you go. Access is by pavement to the end of Teanaway Road and then gravel Forest Road 9737 for the last several miles; the surface is rough enough to want patience in a low car, holds snow into early summer, and washboards badly by August. Beverly is roughly four miles up the gravel and De Roux about eight, with Esmeralda a mile beyond that. If you do want to sleep high for the South Ridge, the designated sites in Headlight Basin are the legal option and camping is prohibited at Ingalls Lake itself; expect the goats there, which are bold, unbothered by people and interested in anything salty, so relieve yourself well away from camp and do not leave sweaty gear out.
bivy.water: No potable water at either campground, so bring what you need. The North Fork Teanaway River runs alongside and is easy to filter from.
bivy.permit: No wilderness permit at all, and nothing to do with the Enchantment lottery. Both campgrounds charge a modest per-night fee paid on site. Roadside dispersed camping is legal on National Forest ground along Forest Road 9737 but is NOT permitted inside the Teanaway Community Forest lower down the valley, where camping is confined to its designated campgrounds. Fire restrictions are common here from midsummer and are taken seriously; this valley is dry and burns. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park at Esmeralda the next morning.
bivy.capacity: Beverly holds around fourteen small tent sites; De Roux is smaller still. Both are first come, first served with no reservations. Dispersed pullouts along the road hold many more parties informally.

wa_argonaut_peak_east_ridge.notes: From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead at the end of the North Fork Teanaway road, take the trail to Longs Pass at about 6,200 ft and drop roughly 1,400 ft to Ingalls Creek. Then follow the Ingalls Creek trail east, downstream, to the camps below Argonaut's south side and climb from there.

wa_bread_loaf.name: Silver Falls loop from the Ohanapecosh side
wa_bread_loaf.notes:
This is a single roadside boulder at about 1,900 ft in old forest, not an alpine objective, and the approach is a walk on maintained trail with essentially no gain.

From the Ohanapecosh day-use area, follow the Silver Falls Loop about a mile. Check which end of the loop is open rather than assuming either.

The road serving this corner of the park is seasonal: normally open from late spring through fall and gated in winter.

No climbing permit is involved. The park's climbing permit and its blue-bag rules apply to parties travelling on glaciers or above 10,000 ft, which this is not; the park entrance fee still applies.
wa_bread_loaf.season: Roughly late spring through fall, whenever the southeast corner of the park is open to vehicles
hazards: Nothing alpine; the real risks are trail closures and construction in this corner of the park
Landing on forest floor with roots and uneven ground
Seasonal road closure to the southeast entrance in winter
wa_bread_loaf.baseFinding:
The test is that you never leave the trail. The boulder sits a few feet off the Silver Falls Loop, roughly a mile round from the Ohanapecosh day-use area. If you have stepped off maintained tread, started bushwhacking, or gained more than about a hundred feet, you have walked past it — go back rather than searching uphill.

The shape is the name: a low boulder with a loaf-shaped top hold, climbed on its left side. One problem, a couple of moves.

The strongest negative is about the whole outing rather than the last hundred yards, and it is worth stating because this route is filed under the mountain: if you are on snow, on a glacier, or anywhere above a few thousand feet, you are not near this boulder and never will be. It is in low forest in the southeast corner of the park, tens of miles and twelve thousand feet from the summit routes filed beside it.

Water and escape are non-problems here — the loop has running water nearby and you can walk out either way round it. That is the honest description; do not carry mountain planning onto it.

wa_bread_loaf.name: Eastside Trail from the Grove of the Patriarchs lot

wa_bread_loaf.notes: Park at the Grove of the Patriarchs lot on the Stevens Canyon Road, cross the road to the Eastside Trail and follow it about half a mile to the Silver Falls Trail, then continue south toward the falls; the boulder is a few feet off the trail. This is the way in whenever the campground end of the loop is closed, and during that closure the loop cannot be walked through, so come back the way you went. The Grove itself stays closed behind its damaged bridge, but the lot and the Eastside Trail are open in season. The loop can also be picked up from this end, and that corridor has been under reconstruction in recent seasons.

wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.name: North Fork Entiat to the Pyramid Mountain junction, then the basin between Saska and Emerald
camps: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
Fox Camp, North Fork Entiat trail
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.notes:
From the North Fork Entiat River Trailhead near 3,940 ft at the end of FR-5606, take Trail #1437 upstream on a gentle grade — only about 1,300 ft of gain over six miles. The lower miles run through old burn and blowdown, so plan on working over and around deadfall rather than walking clean tread. Grouse Creek has been crossed on a logjam roughly 100 ft upstream of the trail crossing, or on a deteriorating footbridge, depending on the year.

Bear right at the Fern Lake fork and stay on #1437. Around mile 7 the trail swings sharply east and switchbacks half a mile to its end at the Pyramid Mountain Trail junction. In early season the tread gets hard to follow once snow patches start above roughly 4,800 ft.

Leave the maintained trail at the junction and head west; the timber opens into a clearing within about a quarter mile. Fill and treat water there — the valley bottom is the last easy water and there is little of it above.

From the clearing the travel is cross-country: angle west then south-west, contouring below Cardinal Peak's west side toward the basin system south of Emerald. Expect to give back 200-300 ft to skirt cliff bands before regaining the open basin floor around 6,900 ft. A camp flat sits near 7,000-7,100 ft.
wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.season: Mid-Jul-Sep for snow-free scrambling; late May and June need an axe and crampons for neve in the summit gullies. October is popular for larch colour and brings short days
hazards: Unmaintained, log-choked trail sections from past wildfire damage on the lower six miles
Grouse Creek crossing by logjam
Loose rock and choss in the summit gullies; several similar gully and bench variations do not all go

wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.baseFinding:
The start of the climbing is the upper basin wedged between Saska and Emerald, and the thing that leads you into it is running water. From the 6,900 ft basin, cross a shoulder near 7,100 ft and climb a gully system into that upper basin. The slabby watercourse draining it gives the most continuous line and holds snow well into early summer — so in cloud, follow the drainage uphill rather than picking a gully by eye.

The arrival is a bench at about 7,800 ft beneath the south-east side of the summit ridge. From there several scramble lines look much alike and none is obviously better than the rest. That is the honest state of this route and it is why the rule below is a direction rather than a description.

The rule is: work up and to climbers' right to stay on the standard line. Right, from the bench. If you have drifted left you are on one of the variations that this face is full of, and they do not all go.

What the correct gully does at its top, which is the confirmation: it tops out at a notch in the summit ridge, and from that notch it is only a short Class 2-3 scramble to the top — one described account calls it a very short Class 3 scramble near the top. So the test is proportion: if you have topped out of a gully and there is a great deal of climbing still above you, you are in the wrong gully.

The summit is two points about 100 ft apart and the north one is the true, marginally higher top. The south point is a noticeably steeper inclined slab and a slip off it runs down the east face. The whole summit area is small and drops away within a few paces in most directions, and several nearby lower rock points can be mistaken for the summit — so the exposure, not the difficulty, is what deserves attention at the top.

What this route is not: it is not a ridge climb despite the name. The name describes the ridge and notch it gains relative to Cardinal Peak, which sits just to the south-east. The climbing is a gully and a short scramble.

wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.name: Emerald Park and Milham Pass from Lucerne

bivy.name: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
bivy.notes: The high camp for the crest traverse, about a mile and a half beyond Fox Camp on the Pyramid trail, in the basin that separates Emerald Peak from Saska Peak. This is where a party stages to link Cardinal, Emerald, Saska and Pinnacle Mountain in a single push over Milham Pass at about 6,663 ft, which is the classic way to do these four and much the most efficient. From the basin you climb to the upper shelf just below the ridge between Emerald and Saska and pick up the broad gully to the summit. Cardinal is the highest of the group and the furthest, and it is the one that turns a two-day plan into three. The setting is superb and the ground is loose — expect scree and blocky scrambling rather than clean rock, and expect the descents to take longer than the ascents. Season is short at this height in a heavy year, realistically mid-July to early October, and the reason to come late is the larch and the reason not to is the water. Weigh that honestly: an August party that finds the tarns dry has a long, hot walk back down to fix it. Weather moves in from the west with little warning here and the basin is fully exposed.
bivy.water: Snowmelt tarns and rivulets in the basin, and these are the crux of the whole plan. They are dependable in early and mid summer, unreliable by mid-August, and in a dry year they are gone entirely by late August, at which point the nearest certain water is back down at Fox Camp. Do not commit to a high camp here in late season without either confirming water or carrying it up. Milham Pass itself has none.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue, party limit of twelve. Camp on durable ground and well back from the tarns. No campfires — forest-wide restrictions aside, there is no fuel at this elevation and the ground is fragile. Reached only through trails inside the Little Giant Fire closure area (Okanogan-Wenatchee order 06-17-07-2026-40), in effect September 3 through October 31, 2026 unless lifted sooner.
bivy.capacity: A small number of tent-sized spots on benches and moraine in the upper basin; two or three parties at most, and less if you want flat ground

wa_emerald_peak_se_ridge.notes: Take the boat up Lake Chelan to Lucerne, follow the Domke Lake trail and fork onto the Emerald Park trail, climbing along Emerald Park Creek to the Emerald Park meadows. Continue about two miles to Milham Pass and drop into the basin between Emerald and Saska, where the ridge begins. It depends on the boat schedule, but it is the natural choice when coming from the Lake Chelan side or linking peaks along the crest.
