wa_gunsight_peak_standard.name: Chickamin Glacier to the snow finger between the main and south spires
camps: Chikamin Glacier bench below the west face
wa_gunsight_peak_standard.notes: From the Chikamin-Dome col, a descending traverse of roughly ninety minutes drops onto the Chickamin Glacier and reaches a snow dome and rock outcrop at about 7,000 ft, closely below the peak; many parties move camp here or day-climb from the col. From that outcrop, boot up to the snow finger running between the main spire and the south spire. On the snow approach, take the first col south of the south peak — the long-standing published advice to use the second col south of it has been corrected by parties who followed it, and the first is the right one. Descent reverses the line by rappel: from the top of the chimney, traverse to the notch, downclimb to a second station, rappel to the ledge above the glacier, then one more onto the snow.
hazards: Crevasses on the Dome and Chikamin Glaciers, with the Chikamin crossing done to and from the base of the climb; hairline to open late season
Descending traverse from the Chikamin-Dome col onto the Chikamin Glacier bench below the west face needs a rope
Loose rock in the basalt dike and upper gully; the dike is softer than the granite around it
Exposed narrow summit ridge, and a barstool-sized summit horn that holds one climber at a time
Gendarmed multi-summit ridge: route-finding errors are easy in cloud or fog
Over 7,000 ft of gain and a multi-day approach from Downey Creek: no cell coverage, self-rescue only
Rappel descent in two double-rope stages; natural anchors only, black dihedral rock loose in spots
wa_gunsight_peak_standard.baseFinding: A reddish-black basalt dike is the line, and it is softer than everything around it. From the 7,000 ft snow dome and rock outcrop, boot up the snow finger between the main and south spires; from a breach in that finger, a short wall leads to a broad ledge, then leftward to a steep dihedral of black rock whose top fifteen feet is the exposed 5.6 crux on solid granite. Above it, traverse left on Class 3 granite into a distinctive dike of reddish-black basalt — this is the feature that carved the gunsight notch in the first place, eroding faster than the granite either side, so if the rock you are on is the same colour as its neighbours you are not in the dike. It scrambles easily, if loosely, to the high notch between the main and north spires. There a vertical headwall blocks a direct exit: descend about twenty feet and traverse right across steep, solid, well-broken rock into a shallow parallel gully. Short chimneys and cracks to 5.5 end at the crest beside a large horn slung with old rappel tat — that horn is not the summit; the summit is a separate horn about the size of a barstool further along the ridge.

wa_gunsight_peak_standard.name: Stehekin, Agnes Creek and Spruce Creek

bivy.name: Chikamin Glacier bench below the west face
bivy.notes: Planned advanced camp, about ninety minutes of descending traverse below the col and directly under Gunsight's west face. Parties move here to shorten summit day rather than day-climbing from the col. It is a glacier bench: rope up moving to and from it, site the tent clear of the fall line off the face, and expect a cold, fully exposed pitch.
bivy.water: snowmelt only
bivy.capacity: small — a snow dome and rock outcrop, a tent or two

wa_gunsight_peak_standard.notes: Take the boat to Stehekin and the shuttle to High Bridge, then hike south on the Pacific Crest Trail up Agnes Creek about ten miles to the Spruce Creek confluence. Cross Agnes Creek and Spruce Creek on logs and scramble northwest to a high camp near Icy-Spruce Creek pass, then cross onto the Chickamin Glacier for the standard line. Expect a long off-trail day with real bushwhacking.
hazards: Long boat-and-shuttle approach: Stehekin boat, then a road shuttle to High Bridge, so a fixed schedule on both ends
About ten miles up Agnes Creek on the Pacific Crest Trail, then off-trail with real bushwhacking to Spruce Creek
Log crossings of Agnes Creek and Spruce Creek
Crevasse hazard on the Chickamin Glacier; rope up moving to and from the glacier bench camp below the west face
Glacier bench camp is cold and fully exposed; site the tent clear of the fall line off the face
Loose rock in the basalt dike and an exposed summit ridge with a one-at-a-time summit horn
Extremely remote: no cell coverage, self-rescue only

wa_liberty_cap_liberty_ridge_finish.name: White River, St. Elmo Pass and the Carbon Glacier
camps: Curtis Ridge / Carbon Glacier access bivy
Lower Curtis Ridge / Carbon Glacier camp
wa_liberty_cap_liberty_ridge_finish.notes: Everyone walks in from White River Campground, and the walking is over quickly. The Glacier Basin Trail is maintained for about three and a half miles to the basin at roughly 5,900 ft, which holds the last running water you will see until the descent brings you down to Camp Schurman. Above the basin there is no trail: a boot track climbs snow and scree to St. Elmo Pass at about 7,400 ft, and from the far side of the pass you drop onto the Winthrop Glacier and stay roped for the rest of the trip. The counter-clockwise traverse under Mount Ruth and around the toe of Curtis Ridge is the part that decides the day, because it runs directly beneath Willis Wall and both walls shed rock and ice more freely once the sun is on them. Most parties split the approach with a bivy on lower Curtis Ridge somewhere between about 7,200 and 7,600 ft, right beside the ramp that drops onto the Carbon Glacier, and it is the only place on the whole approach where you get a head-on look at the route to pick your line. Curtis Ridge is broad and deceptive in cloud and parties repeatedly think they have arrived when they have not; the rule everyone repeats is to stay low and, when in doubt, angle down and right. If what you are looking over is not a mellow fifty-foot talus slope, you are too high, and climbing further only cliffs you out. A climbing permit is required and this line carries its own briefing, so sort both before driving up rather than on the morning you want to leave.
hazards: Rockfall and icefall off Willis Wall onto the Carbon Glacier traverse, worsening as the day warms
Serac collapse off the Liberty Cap Glacier onto the west side of the Carbon basin
Crevasses and thin snow bridges on the Winthrop and Carbon crossings; a slip on the Winthrop traverse can mean a long fall
The moat where glacier meets rock at the foot of the ridge can turn parties around
Rockfall into Thumb Rock camp from the tower opposite
Sustained steep ice to about 60 degrees above the Black Pyramid; summit bergschrund crossing
Altitude, and no retreat down the route once above Thumb Rock
wa_liberty_cap_liberty_ridge_finish.baseFinding: Coming off Curtis Ridge everything underfoot is glacier, so the ridge has to be picked out by shape and by what stands either side of it. Where Liberty Ridge meets the Carbon it is a rock nose, a prow of broken volcanic rock at roughly 8,450 to 8,600 ft rather than a snow slope, and often the place you can watch rocks peeling off. Memorise the compass check, because it holds everywhere on the climb. Facing uphill, Willis Wall is on your left, to the east, and the Liberty Wall is on your right, to the west. If the big wall is on your right hand as you look up, you are on the wrong feature. Cross the Carbon up climber's right of the main icefall and aim for the nose. The real crux of the approach is the moat where the glacier pulls away from the rock, and parties are stopped here more often than anywhere else on the climb — not because the ridge is hard to see, but because there is no way across the gap that day. You can gain the crest from either flank or straight up the toe, at roughly 8,600 to 8,800 ft. The east flank is steeper and carries more rock bands, so most parties cross onto the west flank as soon as they are on the crest and stay there up to camp. Which side actually goes is decided by the moat and the crevasses rather than by preference, so scout instead of committing to the first weakness. In poor visibility the confirmation is not at the toe at all, it is above it: Thumb Rock, a 300 ft gendarme of broken volcanic rock at somewhere around 10,500 ft, with a second loose tower opposite it and barely room for two small tents in the saddle between. Parties fogged out at the base have started to retreat and turned around again only when Thumb Rock showed through a break in the cloud, so if you are unsure, wait for a window and look up rather than along. You have gone too far west if the ground opens into the Carbon basin beneath the Liberty Wall's hanging ice; crevasses routinely push parties that way, and the next spine past that wall is Ptarmigan Ridge, a different climb off a different camp.

wa_liberty_cap_liberty_ridge_finish.name: Carbon River and the Wonderland Trail to Curtis Ridge

bivy.name: Thumb Rock
bivy.notes: Planned high camp and the standard one — flat, partly wind-sheltered tent sites tucked behind the rock buttress, reached by moderate snow and loose rock bands. Reports place the platforms anywhere from about 10,400 to 10,700 ft depending on which bench and how much snow is in; the ground above the rock is more exposed and takes the full wind. There is no liquid water at any point. The approach ramps immediately below turn loose and unpleasant once they melt out, so late-season parties arrive slower than they plan.
bivy.water: none — melt snow or ice
bivy.permit: climbing permit required above 10,000 ft in addition to the camping permit
bivy.capacity: a handful of existing snow platforms; can be crowded in season, and late parties dig their own

bivy.name: Curtis Ridge / Carbon Glacier access bivy
bivy.notes: Planned intermediate camp, and the usual way to split what is otherwise a 7-10 hour push from the car to Thumb Rock. Established sites sit in the ramp that gains the Carbon at about 7,300 ft, with more ground on the ridge crest above. Parties camp here specifically so they can cross the exposed ground under Willis Wall early and cold. Do not pitch out on the open Carbon under the wall to shorten the morning — that is the fall line for serac collapse off the summit icecap.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.capacity: a few small sites in the access gully and on the ridge

bivy.name: Camp Schurman
bivy.notes: Descent camp. Liberty Ridge tops out near Liberty Cap and most parties come down the Emmons-Winthrop, so this is where a slow summit day ends rather than a forced night out high on the ice. Ranger hut and solar toilet, both potentially buried in snow — carry blue bags and pack them out. Reserve well ahead.
bivy.water: none — melt snow
bivy.permit: wilderness camping permit required; separate climbing permit for glacier travel
bivy.capacity: limited designated tent sites; fills early in season

bivy.name: Lower Curtis Ridge / Carbon Glacier camp

wa_liberty_cap_liberty_ridge_finish.notes: The older way in, used mainly early in the season when the White River road is still closed. From the Carbon River entrance, walk or bike the old road to Ipsut Creek, then follow the Wonderland Trail up the Carbon River to the snout of the Carbon Glacier and onto the ice toward Curtis Ridge. It starts lower and is noticeably longer than the White River approach, and the Carbon River crossing on the Wonderland Trail can be a problem.
hazards: Long approach from the Carbon River entrance: old road, then the Wonderland Trail up the Carbon River
Carbon River crossing on the Wonderland Trail can be a problem
Travel up the Carbon Glacier snout toward Curtis Ridge: crevasses and thin snow bridges
Rockfall and icefall off Willis Wall; do not camp on the open Carbon under the wall
Serac collapse off the Liberty Cap Glacier; the moat at the foot of the ridge
Sustained steep ice to about 60 degrees above the Black Pyramid; summit bergschrund crossing
Altitude, and no retreat down the route once above Thumb Rock

wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.name: Smithbrook Trail and the crest trail to Lake Valhalla
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.notes: From the Smithbrook Trailhead on the gravel spur off the highway, climb the signed Smithbrook Trail through nearly twenty short switchbacks to Union Gap, where it meets the crest trail; the summit is in view to the south for much of that stretch once the forest opens. Turn left and follow the crest trail south, contouring below the mountain's east flank through a mix of forest and open heather meadow and crossing Smith Brook, which is a reliable place to filter before leaving the trail. Where the trail bends away from Lake Valhalla, drop off it down a steep dirt path to the water and follow the rocky shoreline round to the lake's south tip.
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.season: Snow-free ground roughly July through October; the same slopes are skinned or snowshoed as a separate winter tour. The access road is unplowed in winter and typically melts out by early to mid summer.
hazards: No trail beyond the lake outlet; real tread only reappears on the summit ridge
More than one gully on this side of the mountain and only the middle one is the route
The peak visible from the lake is a lower sub-summit; parties have climbed it by mistake onto slick class 4 and 5 ground
Short cliff bands that force backtracking
Loose talus and scree in the gully with rockfall onto anyone below
The gully often holds snow into early summer; firm morning snow
Afternoon thunderstorms on the open ridge
wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.baseFinding: When faced with a choice of gullies, take the middle one — and know that the peak you can see is not the summit. From the southeast area of the lake begin a slight ascent to the southeast, looking for the obvious rock-filled gully. Be careful here: there is more than one gully on this side of the mountain, and the middle of them is the route. Ascend it to where it terminates, then work around the first small cliff band to the left, on its north side. Above that, climb right toward a gentle saddle; from the saddle a traverse northeast is the easier finish, while going northwest is the exposed option and is not the ordinary line. The wrong-place marker is the thing you have been looking at all along: from the lake the true summit is hidden, and what stands in front of it is a smaller unnamed peak that looks steep and sketchy. Parties have climbed toward it by mistake and turned back a few metres short on slick class 4 and 5 rock. There is no trail at all beyond the lake outlet, so finding none is expected; real tread reappears only on the summit ridge.

wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.name: Crest trail north from Stevens Pass

bivy.name: Lake Valhalla
bivy.notes: The natural base for both Lichtenberg Mountain and Mount McCausland, which stand on opposite sides of the bowl the lake fills. Lichtenberg's broad face rises straight out of the water on the south side and is the peak everyone photographs from camp; McCausland is the gentler summit to the northeast, gained by a signed spur off the Pacific Crest Trail a little under three miles from the Smithbrook trailhead and reachable from camp in about an hour. The short way in is Smithbrook Road to the trailhead, then a mile or so of switchbacks to Union Gap and a traverse south on the Pacific Crest Trail, roughly five miles each way. The long way is the Pacific Crest Trail north from the pass itself, about five and a half miles with less climbing but more distance. Thru-hiker traffic through July and August adds real pressure on a small number of sites, so arrive early or plan to camp away from the water. Season is roughly mid-July through October; snow lingers in this bowl and the trail is muddy for weeks after it goes. In winter Smithbrook Road is unplowed and the approach lengthens considerably, which is why the winter ascents of Lichtenberg come at it from the road rather than from the lake.
bivy.water: The lake itself, and a small inlet at the south end. Wash and rinse well back from the shore — this is a small basin carrying a lot of traffic.
bivy.permit: Henry M. Jackson Wilderness. A free self-issue permit is filled out at the trailhead register. A Northwest Forest Pass is required at the Smithbrook trailhead; the Pacific Crest Trail lot at Stevens Pass needs no pass but does need the self-registration. Campfires are prohibited at the lake — carry a stove.
bivy.capacity: A handful of established sites scattered around the lake, mostly in the trees on the north and east shores, plus a couple of backcountry toilets. First come, first served, and genuinely full on summer weekends.

approachLogistics.trailhead: Stevens Pass North Lot (crest trail northbound)

wa_lichtenberg_mountain_se_route.notes: Park in the north lot at Stevens Pass and pick up the crest trail heading north from behind the maintenance buildings. It contours the slopes above Nason Creek and reaches Lake Valhalla from the west, where you leave the trail and work around the lake to the scramble. It is a few miles longer than the Smithbrook start but needs no gravel road, and it is the usual start when Smith Brook road is under snow.
hazards: Long start from Stevens Pass along the crest trail, a few miles longer than the Smithbrook start
No trail beyond the lake: leave the crest trail on arrival and work around the lake to the scramble
Unmaintained, overgrown boot path along the lake's west shore
More than one gully on this side and the true summit is hidden behind a lower sub-summit that parties climb by mistake
Short cliff bands that can cliff out parties climbing directly toward the summit
Loose talus and scree in the gully with rockfall onto anyone below; lingering snow in the gully
Afternoon thunderstorms on the open ridge

wa_lincoln_peak_standard.name: Middle Fork Nooksack Road (FR-38) and Rankin Creek to the treeline camp, then the southwest basin
wa_lincoln_peak_standard.notes:
This is the more direct way to the X Couloir: from the south via the Middle Fork Nooksack River Road (FR-38). The southwest face can also be reached by a less direct line with more glacier travel; do not confuse either with the north-facing Coleman side, which leads to the other route on this mountain.

Drive FR-38 toward its mile-12.5 switchback and start walking the old decommissioned road around Point 4481 toward Rankin Creek. Snow travel — often by bike or snowshoe on the lower stretch — leads past East Rankin Lake near 5,120 ft and up into the basin to a sheltered camp at treeline around 6,100 ft, by the highest trees in the basin below Seward Peak. Roughly seven miles and 3,350 ft of gain to camp.

Access: FR-38, damaged in the December 2025 floods, has been closed to vehicles at milepost 7 by a washout since July 27, 2026, with no end date given on the Mt. Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest alert still posted on September 26, 2026, and a separate gate at Wallace Creek near mile 10 closes the road 1 December to 15 June for elk calving. Confirm the drivable road-end with the Mount Baker Ranger District before the trip; the length of the approach varies year to year.
wa_lincoln_peak_standard.season: Roughly Apr-Jun. A spring snow climb; essentially never done in summer, because what makes it climbable is continuous snow rather than the rubble underneath
hazards: FR-38 flood damage with no repair timeline, plus an elk-calving gate closed 1 Dec to 15 Jun, so the approach length varies
Bergschrund crossing (AI3+ on 70-85 degree snow and ice) that must be done cold and early
About 1,500 ft of 30-40 degree snow with a steep serac step, all above a long runout
Notoriously loose, rotten volcanic rock; the gully funnels rockfall and spindrift after storms
Wet-snow instability and rapid softening on the southwest-facing line as it warms
Descent is a real rappel sequence off pickets and slung horns, not a walk-off
Complex route-finding among the Black Buttes
wa_lincoln_peak_standard.baseFinding:
The highest trees in the basin are the camp, and the camp is the last thing you can navigate to. Above treeline the southwest side of Lincoln is open snow and there is nothing to hold on to in cloud. So the arrival marker is vegetative rather than topographic: climb until the trees stop, and camp at the last of them, below Seward Peak, around 6,100 ft.

The bergschrund is the base of the climb. From camp an alpine start takes you into the southwest basin and to the schrund while the snow is still cold and firm. Above it is roughly 1,500 ft of 30-40 degree snow with a steep serac step in it.

Do not expect one clean couloir — this is the trap the name sets. Parties who have climbed and skied it describe it as less a couloir and more a series of steep chutes and faces, and the line drops from the high point to the highest notch, then down a narrow chute, and trends right out of view. So 'find the obvious couloir' is the wrong instruction and will have you standing in the basin looking for something that is not there. Work from the notch downward: the correct line is the one that connects to the highest notch on the skyline, and it is narrow where it leaves the basin.

The serac step is the confirmation. Somewhere in that 1,500 ft you meet a steep serac step. A line with no ice step in it is not the X Couloir.

And the aspect settles the coarse error: this route faces southwest and this approach reaches it from Rankin Creek. If you are standing on the Coleman Glacier looking at a shaded north-facing cirque, you are under the other route on this mountain.

wa_lincoln_peak_standard.name: Heliotrope Ridge and the Thunder Glacier cirque
wa_lincoln_peak_standard.notes: Start at the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead and follow the trail toward the old cabin site, then rope up and cross the lower glaciers south into the Thunder Glacier cirque to reach the southwest side of the peak. It is less direct than the Rankin Creek line, with much more glacier travel, but it starts from a paved-to-gravel road that is usually open when the Middle Fork road is not.
hazards: Roped glacier travel across the lower glaciers into the Thunder Glacier cirque, with more glacier travel than the Rankin Creek line
Crevasse and serac hazard on the approach glaciers
Bergschrund crossing (AI3+ on 70-85 degree snow and ice) that must be done cold and early
About 1,500 ft of 30-40 degree snow with a steep serac step above a long runout
Notoriously loose, rotten volcanic rock; the gully funnels rockfall and spindrift after storms
Wet-snow instability and rapid softening on the southwest-facing line as it warms
Descent is a real rappel sequence; going back north toward Heliotrope Ridge from a Rankin camp puts a glacier between you and camp

wa_mount_adams_mazama_glacier_headwall.name: Bird Creek Meadows and Sunrise Camp, on the Yakama Reservation side
wa_mount_adams_mazama_glacier_headwall.notes:
This is the southeast side of the mountain and the approach crosses Yakama Nation land, which makes it an access problem before it is a climbing problem. A tribal-use permit for Tract D is required, bought at the fee station on entry at the Mirror Lake gate — it cannot be obtained in advance — and it is only available when the area is open to non-tribal use. The Yakama Nation sets that window for non-members each year, somewhere between July and early autumn. The area has also been closed outright in some years, so confirm with the Yakama Nation before building a trip around this approach; there is no alternative way in from this side.

From the Bird Creek Meadows parking area (about 5,576–5,700 ft), the trail is easy to follow to roughly 6,700 ft. Above that it is route-finding: any number of lines through moraine, scree and glacier remnants lead up to Sunrise Camp at about 8,300 ft. Carry a map — locating the camp is the part people get wrong. Trailhead to camp is about 3–4 hours.

Sunrise Camp sits at the base of the Mazama Glacier, tucked between the glacier and a small rock hill, with hand-built rock shelters. It is a fine fair-weather camp and a poor one otherwise: it is exposed to winds that can reach hurricane strength, and to rockfall off the glacier. The rock walls help, but only somewhat.

From camp to summit is about 5 hours.
wa_mount_adams_mazama_glacier_headwall.season: Summer; non-tribal access to this side has historically been limited to a mid-summer to early-autumn window
hazards: Tribal-use permit required, sold only at the gate in a limited seasonal window; no advance purchase and closed in some years
Route-finding through moraine and scree above 6,700 ft to locate Sunrise Camp
Rockfall off the glacier onto Sunrise Camp
Extreme wind exposure at camp
Crevasses on the Mazama Glacier and bergschrunds around 9,500 ft
Steep optional exit variation near the top
Mistaking Piker's Peak, where the route tops out, for the true summit
wa_mount_adams_mazama_glacier_headwall.baseFinding:
The climbing starts directly above camp — the first ground you cross after leaving Sunrise Camp is the glacier itself, so the recognition problem here is finding camp, not finding the base.

Sunrise Camp: at roughly 8,300 ft, a flat with rock wind shelters, wedged between the toe of the Mazama Glacier on one side and a small rock hill on the other. If you are on open moraine with no rock hill beside you, you are short of it or off to one side; the terrain between 6,700 and 8,300 ft has many plausible lines and only some of them end at the camp.

Above camp the sequence is legible. Long stretches of glacier at about 40 degrees, then bear right onto the headwall proper, which runs about 45 degrees and is where pickets earn their place. Bergschrunds appear around 9,500 ft. The glacier narrows as it climbs.

The top is where the route makes you choose. Nearing Piker's Peak — the south summit at 11,644 ft — you can exit left onto easy 25–30 degree ground, or stay right for a short technical finish: roughly 40 ft of 60–70 degree snow and ice on the southeast corner, worth two or three screws.

Critical negative marker at the top: Piker's Peak is not the summit of Mount Adams. When the ground flattens out you have reached the south summit; the true summit is a further dome across the plateau to the north, with the geographic high point to the east. This route tops out on the false summit by design, so treat the flattening as a halfway signal rather than an arrival.

wa_mount_adams_mazama_glacier_headwall.name: Cold Springs and the Round the Mountain trail
wa_mount_adams_mazama_glacier_headwall.notes: From the Cold Springs trailhead, climb the South Climb trail to the Round the Mountain trail and follow it east across the lava flows to the reservation boundary and the edge of Bird Creek Meadows, then turn uphill onto the moraine toward the Mazama Glacier and Sunrise Camp. The turnoff is farther along the Round the Mountain trail than many descriptions suggest. A Recreation Pass is needed at Cold Springs.
hazards: Long approach across lava flows on the Round the Mountain trail; the moraine turnoff is farther along than many descriptions suggest
Recreation pass and tribal-use permit rules apply entering Yakama land; area closed in some years
Route-finding through moraine and scree to locate Sunrise Camp
Rockfall off the glacier onto Sunrise Camp, extreme wind at camp
Crevasses on the Mazama Glacier and bergschrunds around 9,500 ft
Steep optional exit variation near the top; Piker's Peak can be mistaken for the summit

wa_mount_adams_mount_adams_circumnavigat.name: Start and finish at Killen Creek
wa_mount_adams_mount_adams_circumnavigat.notes: Climb the Killen Creek trail to the crest trail and the Highline trail, then go around the east side of the mountain off trail, cross the untrailed gap on the Yakama side, and return along the Round the Mountain trail and the crest trail. The gap is open only a few weeks a year and needs glacier skills and route finding.
hazards: Trailless east-side stretch (about 4-5 miles, 'The Gap') crossing the Mazama, Klickitat and Rusk glaciers
Unstable moraine and talus on the gap crossing
Glacial rivers such as the Big Muddy to cross
Gap open only a few weeks a year; needs glacier skills and route-finding
East side is Yakama Nation land: permit required and the area can be closed

wa_mount_adams_mount_adams_circumnavigat.name: Start and finish at Cold Springs
wa_mount_adams_mount_adams_circumnavigat.notes: Start on the South Climb trail from Cold Springs and climb steeply toward Sunrise Camp, then circle the mountain mostly between 7,000 and 8,000 ft across many glaciers and moraines, picking up the Round the Mountain trail east of Horseshoe Meadows to return. It is a little shorter than the Killen Creek start.
hazards: Steep climb on the South Climb trail from Cold Springs toward Sunrise Camp
Circuit mostly between 7,000 and 8,000 ft across many glaciers and moraines
Unstable moraine and glacial river crossings on the east side
Trailless Gap on the Yakama side open only a few weeks a year; needs glacier skills and route-finding
East side is Yakama Nation land: permit required and the area can be closed

wa_mount_baker_cockscomb_ridge.name: Heliotrope Ridge, the Hogsback and the Coleman-Roosevelt crossing
wa_mount_baker_cockscomb_ridge.notes:
Glacier Creek Road (FR 39) to the Heliotrope Ridge trailhead, then Trail 677 through old growth to the fork at about two miles. Take the right-hand climbers' path up the crest of the Hogsback moraine to the camps near 6,000 ft beside the Coleman Glacier, the same camp used for the Coleman-Deming and the North Ridge.

From camp the route ropes up and heads northeast, crossing the Coleman and then the Roosevelt Glacier. Expect two to three hours of glacier travel through a crevasse field before low-to-moderate snow ramps lead to the foot of the ridge.
hazards: Crevasses and thin snow bridges on the Coleman and Roosevelt Glaciers
Bergschrunds below and on the ridge
Loose rock on the ridge, worse as the snow melts out
Icefall on the ramps that skirt the towers
Rockfall potential below the Cockscomb Tower
Late-season detour onto the Park Glacier and its AI3 headwall may be needed to bypass the Tower
wa_mount_baker_cockscomb_ridge.baseFinding:
The ridge is reached by traversing northeast from the Hogsback camps across the Coleman and then the Roosevelt Glacier. Aim for the foot of the ridge at about 7,500-7,800 ft, where low-angle snow ramps lead up onto the crest.

The Cockscomb Tower, about 300 ft high, stands well above the base and is passed on its east side by steep snow; if you are already beside it, you are far above the start. If you have crossed only the Coleman and are still west of the Roosevelt, you have not reached this ridge yet.

wa_mount_baker_cockscomb_ridge.name: Artist Point and Ptarmigan Ridge to the Park Glacier

bivy.name: Park Glacier camp near the Portals
bivy.notes: Beyond Camp Kiser, across the Rainbow Glacier and onto the Park Glacier. This is where most parties sleep before the Park Glacier Headwall or the Cockscomb.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only
bivy.permit: No overnight permit required
bivy.capacity: Snow or rock platforms for a few tents

bivy.name: Camp Kiser, Ptarmigan Ridge
bivy.notes: About five miles out Ptarmigan Ridge where the maintained trail ends. A good first night, with the glaciers still to cross.
bivy.water: Snowmelt only; can be dry late in summer
bivy.permit: No overnight permit required
bivy.capacity: Dispersed sites among rock wind walls

wa_mount_baker_cockscomb_ridge.notes: From Artist Point at the end of the Mount Baker Highway, take the Chain Lakes trail to the Ptarmigan Ridge junction and follow Ptarmigan Ridge west to Camp Kiser where the trail ends. Cross the Rainbow Glacier onto the Park Glacier and camp near the Portals, the usual base for the Cockscomb from this side. It is a much longer approach than Heliotrope Ridge.
hazards: Rainbow and Park Glacier crossings, crevassed, from Camp Kiser
Much longer approach: Chain Lakes trail, Ptarmigan Ridge to Camp Kiser, then onto the glacier
Bergschrunds below and on the ridge
Loose rock on the ridge, worse as the snow melts out
Icefall on the ramps that skirt the towers
Rockfall potential below the Cockscomb Tower; late-season Park Glacier AI3 headwall bypass of the Tower

wa_mount_crowder_southwest_route.name: Hannegan Pass, Easy Ridge and Perfect Pass, then south along the west side of the range to the Phantom-Crowder col
camps: Easy Ridge bivouac ground below Easy Peak
Perfect Pass, Perfect Pass cross-country zone
wa_mount_crowder_southwest_route.notes:
From the Hannegan Pass Trailhead the trail climbs about 4 miles to Hannegan Pass, then drops the far side to the Chilliwack River. Ford the river near Easy Creek and climb steeply onto Easy Ridge, then follow its crest over Easy Peak. The Imperfect Impasse, a notch guarded by snow moats and wet, down-sloping slabs, usually has to be passed by dropping several hundred feet and climbing back up exposed class 4 ground. Beyond it, carry on to Perfect Pass.

From Perfect Pass the line stays on the west side of the range and heads south: across the edge of the Challenger Glacier, below Crooked Thumb and Ghost Peak, and along under the west side of Phantom Peak. Keep going south to the col between Phantom and Crowder. It is several days of travel each way, with no shortcut and no easy way out once you are past Easy Ridge.
hazards: Fording the Chilliwack River
The Imperfect Impasse: snow moats, wet down-sloping slabs and an exposed class 4 climb back up
Crevasses wherever the line crosses glacier below Challenger and Crooked Thumb
Whiteout navigation on open snowfields between the Impasse and Perfect Pass
No reasonable retreat once past Easy Ridge; multi-day self-rescue distance

wa_mount_crowder_southwest_route.baseFinding:
The climb starts at the col between Phantom Peak and Crowder, the low point, a little over 6,000 ft, of the ridge that runs south from Phantom. From the col, head southwest and up over a lesser summit of about 7,020 ft. The summit block is beyond it, not on it, and a rib of sound rock leads from its base to the top.

If the rock in front of you is a steep face dropping north toward Picket Creek, you are on the wrong side: Crowder's north side is the steep one, while its west and southwest slopes are moderate.

wa_mount_crowder_southwest_route.notes:
The seldom-used way in, from the west. From the Baker River Trailhead at the end of Baker Lake Road, take the Baker River Trail up the valley, then get up onto Pioneer Ridge and follow the high route along it to the southeast. Pioneer Ridge is a long, rough massif, walled by cliffs and slabs above the Baker River and Picket Creek, and its highest point is at the far southeast end, west of Goodell Creek. Crowder's southwest flank runs down at an easy angle to the foot of that ridge, so this line reaches the peak from below on the southwest rather than at the Phantom col.

Nothing about this line is recorded in detail: no mileage, no gain and no camps. Treat it as a serious cross-country route and plan it from the map. Baker Lake Road has been closed to vehicles and walkers from the Shannon Creek Bridge to the trailhead since mid-July 2026 for construction; check before going.

Climb the North Face (or the Hanging Glacier or the Northwest Rib) to the upper mountain, then continue up the northeast ridge of the summit pyramid. A common way to the foot of the North Face is over Fisher Chimneys and down the White Salmon Glacier to a bivy at its base.

wa_mount_shuksan_northeast_ridge.notes: Climb the Sulphide Glacier to the base of the summit pyramid, then descend a short way east onto the Crystal Glacier and cross it to the foot of the ridge, avoiding a few small crevasses. The ridge is very loose fourth class until the last 200 ft, which is a solid, clean face of low fifth class leading almost to the summit.

wa_mount_stuart_stuart_glacier_couloir.name: Mountaineer Creek to the basin, then west onto the Stuart Glacier
wa_mount_stuart_stuart_glacier_couloir.notes:
From the Stuart Lake trailhead at the end of Eightmile Road, follow the trail about three miles to the Colchuck Lake turnoff and continue past it for roughly another mile. Where the Stuart Lake trail switchbacks up and to the right, veer left to stay in the main valley — the same leaving point every north-side route on this mountain uses.

Follow the valley about a mile and a half to where it steepens, then turn right and work up the steep slope into the small hanging valley above, the flat basin under the Sherpa and Ice Cliff glaciers at roughly 5,400 ft. Standard camp is here.

From the basin the route continues west, round the far side of the North Ridge, onto the Stuart Glacier. Entry to the couloir is at about 7,800 ft.

The couloir itself runs 40-50 degree snow, narrows to a short steep step whose character depends entirely on the season, then a second shorter step, then opens into a wider snowfield leading to a notch in the West Ridge. Six pitches of mixed ground follow from that notch to the summit.
wa_mount_stuart_stuart_glacier_couloir.season: Best while the couloir holds continuous snow and the steps take ice, roughly late spring into early summer; later the steps go rocky and the climbing turns mixed
hazards: Crevasses on the Stuart Glacier below the couloir
Rockfall and wet-snow avalanche in the couloir as the day warms
Narrow couloir funnels rockfall; bergschrund at the base

Six pitches of mixed climbing above the notch, on the far side of the mountain from camp

wa_mount_stuart_stuart_glacier_couloir.baseFinding: The north ridge rock rib decides it, and the side it is on is the answer. From the basin you are looking at four things in a row: the Sherpa Glacier, the Ice Cliff Glacier, the enormous rock rib of the North Ridge, and beyond it the Stuart Glacier. You want to be past the rib. So: if the North Ridge rib is on your left (east) you are on the Stuart Glacier and correct. If it is still on your right you have not gone far enough west and are on the Ice Cliff side. That is the same test the Ice Cliff Glacier route uses, read in the opposite direction, and it is the reliable one in cloud because it does not depend on seeing the summit. Second test — what the couloir leads to. This couloir does not go to the summit. It goes to a notch in the west ridge, which is on the far side of the mountain from where you camped. If the line you are looking up appears to head for the top of the peak, you are looking at the wrong feature. Third, the shape. Entry is at about 7,800 ft and the couloir narrows above you before it widens again — moderate snow, then a short steep step, then a second shorter one, then an open snowfield. A line that is uniformly wide with no steps is not this one. And the negative test: no hanging ice cliff or serac band should be above you anywhere. If there is one, you are back on the Ice Cliff Glacier, on the wrong side of the rib.

wa_mount_stuart_stuart_glacier_couloir.name: Esmeralda, Ingalls Lake and Stuart Pass to Goat Pass

bivy.name: Goat Pass bivies
bivy.notes: The high camp of choice for the upper North Ridge and the Stuart Glacier Couloir when approaching from the Ingalls side, putting the traverse under the glacier and the entry gully within an easy morning. Bivy ground is plentiful and reasonably flat, but the position is exposed and windy, so bring a shelter rather than counting on a sheltered nook. From here the standard line traverses east below the Stuart Glacier above the moraine, with snow crossings well into summer. The water situation is the binding constraint late in the season — treat it as a dry camp unless you have seen recent conditions.
bivy.water: No dependable running water. Snowmelt trickles and lingering patches are usually workable into midsummer, but by late season the pass is dry and you must carry water up or melt snow off the glacier below
bivy.permit: Reached from the Esmeralda Basin trailhead over Ingalls Pass and Stuart Pass, so approached on Alpine Lakes Wilderness ground under the Cle Elum Ranger District — free self-issued trailhead permit, Northwest Forest Pass to park, no Enchantment lottery permit. The pass sits on the divide, however: a party that continues down into the Mountaineer Creek drainage and camps there is entering the Stuart Zone and needs that overnight permit between May 15 and Oct 31.
bivy.capacity: Numerous small rock-and-gravel platforms along the pass; several independent parties can spread out without crowding each other

wa_mount_stuart_stuart_glacier_couloir.notes: From the Esmeralda Basin trailhead, hike over Ingalls Pass to Ingalls Lake, then traverse toward Stuart Pass. Near 7,000 ft cross the scree gully north to Goat Pass at about 7,600 ft, where there is plenty of bivy ground. From the pass descend a short way onto the Stuart Glacier and traverse under the North Ridge to the couloir; the glacier passes above some large crevasses.

wa_point_success_south_side.name: Longmire, the Wonderland Trail and Indian Henry's Hunting Ground
camps: Point 6631 (base camp north of Pyramid Peak)
Dug platform on the lower-mid cleaver
wa_point_success_south_side.notes:
Longmire (2,762 ft) is the start, on the Wonderland Trail toward Indian Henry's Hunting Ground. About 3 miles out the trail drops steeply to cross Kautz Creek — a braided glacial outwash channel whose crossing is periodically wrecked by debris flows off the Kautz Glacier. Ask at the Longmire wilderness desk before you leave, because a failed crossing means a long reroute rather than a wet foot.

Beyond Kautz Creek the trail switchbacks through old growth, fords Fisher's Hornpipe Creek and passes Devil's Dream camp (about 5 miles, reliable water) before opening into the meadows of Indian Henry's Hunting Ground at roughly 6.3–7 miles and 5,300 ft, marked by the 1915 patrol cabin.

At Indian Henry's leave the Wonderland for the Mirror Lakes spur — plank walkways over marshy meadow, then the end of maintained tread. The path fades into a boot track at about 5,600 ft in the basin between Copper Peak and Pyramid Peak. From there it is cross-country on the southwest and west slopes of Pyramid Peak, between roughly 6,000 and 6,300 ft, to Point 6631 just north of the peak. Snowmelt water is often available here into early summer, and the rock-slab camp below Pyramid Peak at about 6,300 ft is a common first night.

This is one of only two routes on Rainier that avoids significant glacier travel, which is its whole appeal; the cost is that it is long, loose and unfrequented, with about 12–13 miles and roughly 11,500 ft of gain to Point Success. Most parties take two days, often with a second camp dug into the cleaver crest around 10,700 ft.
wa_point_success_south_side.season: May through September; the lower cleaver is best while it still holds snow, since it becomes loose scree once bare

wa_point_success_south_side.baseFinding:
The climbing starts at the col north of Pyramid Peak, at about 6,400 ft, and getting into that col is where people go wrong.

From Point 6631 you drop north-northeast a short way to a saddle. It is a scree and loose-boulder col, and it is ugly — that is the correct place. There is an easier descent line into it than the obvious one, and trip reports record missing it and taking the worst ground; look for the line before you commit, and note it for the way back.

From the col the cleaver rises continuously in front of you and does not stop. There is no single track and no cairned line: the lower cleaver is loose choss and scree with short bursts of class 3 scrambling, and the route-finding is yours.

The test that you are on the cleaver and not off it is what is on either side. You should be on a broad rubbly crest with the South Tahoma Glacier falling away to your north (climber's left) and the Pyramid and Success glaciers to your south (climber's right). If a glacier is underfoot you have left the cleaver — this route is defined by not being on one.

An easy, clean start is the wrong sign. If the ground out of the col is pleasant walking on solid rock, you are probably contouring around the peak rather than gaining the cleaver. Travel only improves higher, above about 7,000 ft, where the rock firms up and, early in the season, continuous snow and goat tracks take over.

Higher still the crest includes a knife-edge section that needs genuine scrambling once the snow melts off it, and the route then angles climber's right up snow gullies onto the Kautz Cleaver at roughly 12,200–12,600 ft.

The Kautz Creek crossing is periodically damaged by debris flows, so ask about its status before you go.

wa_rock_mountain_west_route.name: Trail #1587 from US-2 to the Nason Ridge crest
wa_rock_mountain_west_route.notes: One of the steepest maintained trails near Stevens Pass, and it starts working immediately. From the dirt pullout on the north side of the highway the tread climbs on an old service road beneath powerlines, leaves the roadbed at a signed bend about a third of a mile up, and then runs into ninety-odd tight switchbacks on an open south-facing slope with no shade at all. Schilling Creek near the bottom is the only accessible water on the climb and it drops away quickly, so fill everything at the car and carry three litres or more. The grade eases into heather meadows around 2.8 miles and the tread tops out on the crest at about 6,000 ft.
wa_rock_mountain_west_route.season: Late June to October; snow lingers
hazards: Ninety-odd tight switchbacks on an open south-facing slope with no shade; heat and sun load
No reliable water above the creek low down; carry 3+ liters

wa_rock_mountain_west_route.baseFinding: Two signed junctions bracket the start of the scrambling and neither is the base by itself. The first is where the trail tops out on the crest at roughly 6,000 ft and meets the Nason Ridge trail; turn left along the ridge here, since the right-hand branch drops away toward a lake overlook. The second, about half a mile on, is where the Snowy Creek trail joins from the south — that is the alternate approach, not your line, and past it the constructed tread stops being tread and thins into a path over loose jumbled talus. That change underfoot is the base. From there the crest runs over a false south summit first; it carries no structure on it. The true summit beyond is identified by the stone foundation of the old fire lookout, and the short connecting ridge between the two is narrow enough to want care and can hold a cornice or old snow into early summer. If you are standing on a high point with nothing built on it and the ridge carries on, keep going.

wa_rock_mountain_west_route.name: Snowy Creek trail from Smith Brook road

bivy.name: Nason Creek Campground and the Lake Wenatchee drive-in camps
bivy.notes: The drive-in base for the whole ridge, and the honest recommendation for most parties climbing these peaks: all four summits are day objectives from the highway trailheads, and sleeping at a developed campground with water and driving fifteen or twenty minutes to a trailhead beats carrying an overnight load up two thousand feet of dry switchbacks. The season runs roughly May through mid-October. From here the Merritt Lake and Round Mountain trailheads are a short drive west and north along the highway and its spurs, with Rock Mountain and Snowy Creek further west toward the pass. It is also the sensible place to reorganise mid-trip: a party that has come off the crest at one end and needs to reposition to the other has this corridor to do it in. Note that the trailheads themselves have very limited parking — Rock Mountain and Snowy Creek in particular hold only a few cars — so an early start from a nearby campground is worth more here than the extra sleep of staying further out.
bivy.water: Piped potable water at the developed campgrounds through the operating season, and Nason Creek itself alongside. This is the one place where water is a non-issue, which is why every party working this ridge should fill everything here before driving up to a trailhead rather than counting on anything above.
bivy.permit: A per-night fee, currently around the high twenties at the forest campground, with advance reservations opening well ahead and closing a few days before arrival. The state park campgrounds have their own reservation system and their own fee. No wilderness permit is involved anywhere in this zone. Fire restrictions apply in the campgrounds through the summer and are commonly total bans in late season.
bivy.capacity: Nason Creek is the closest and largest, laid out over four loops on both sides of the highway near the southeastern end of Lake Wenatchee, taking vehicles up to about thirty-five feet. Roughly sixty percent of sites are reservable in advance and the remainder are first come, first served. The state park campgrounds around the lake add substantially more capacity, and there are further national forest campgrounds spread along the highway corridor.

bivy.name: Rock Lake
bivy.notes: The camp for Rock Mountain and the western anchor of the whole crest. The Rock Mountain trail leaves US 2 at about 2,650 feet and is relentless — roughly 3,400 feet in four miles of endless switchbacks on a hot, open, south-facing slope with no water and very little shade, which is the single most quoted complaint about this peak. The lake sits in a basin below the summit ridge, so a party that has ground up the trail can drop packs, camp, and take the northeast ridge and the summit unencumbered. Most people do Rock Mountain in a day; camping here is what you do when the heat has beaten you, when you are starting the Nason Ridge traverse rather than finishing it, or when you want the summit at first light. The alternative approach by the Snowy Creek trail from the forest road on the north side starts higher and climbs less, and it is the kinder line in warm weather, though the road is brushy. Snow lingers on the upper slopes into early summer and the basin holds it later than the trail below. West of the lake, the crest trail toward Crescent Lake has badly eroded steep sidehill sections with little tread left, and that stretch is the crux of moving along this ridge with a pack.
bivy.water: The lake, and it is the first water of any kind on the Rock Mountain trail — the entire climb from the highway is dry. It holds all season. Treat it, because the shoreline is well used and the basin is small. Fill here for everything you intend to do on the crest, since the next dependable source westward or eastward is Crescent Lake, and the ridge between the two carries nothing.
bivy.permit: None. Nason Ridge sits outside the Alpine Lakes Wilderness, so there is no wilderness permit, no self-issue slip, no quota and no lottery anywhere. The Rock Mountain trailhead has very limited parking, though no fee is charged there and the Merritt Lake end requires no pass either; of the trailheads serving this crest only Nason Ridge is a fee site, at $5 a day or $30 a year. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 feet in this national forest, which covers this camp and every other high site here, and summer burn bans are routine on this dry east-side ground.
bivy.capacity: Several pleasant established sites around the lake, enough for two or three parties; small and it feels small, with no facilities

wa_rock_mountain_west_route.notes: Drive Smith Brook road six miles and the narrow, brushy Snowy Creek road a further three and a half to a small trailhead with very limited parking. The trail follows Snowy Creek through old growth, then climbs to the crest and joins the main route about half a mile short of the summit. It is shorter and far less steep than the highway trail. The Snowy Creek road has been closed by storm damage since June 2026, so check before driving it.

wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.name: North Fork Entiat and the primitive Pyramid Creek Trail to the Emerald-Saska basin
camps: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
Cottonwood Camp and the Entiat River road campgrounds
Fox Camp, North Fork Entiat trail
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.notes: From the North Fork Entiat Trailhead at about 3,940 ft at the end of FR-5606, the first four miles of Trail #1437 climb gently up the valley through old burn, where blowdown and washed-out sections make the going slower than the grade suggests. There is little shade and the valley bottom runs hot and dry — carry water. Continue up-valley another four miles, gaining roughly 3,000 ft from the trailhead, to the Pyramid Creek / Fern Lake junction. That junction is anywhere from seven to nine miles in depending on how far up the road you were able to start. Fox Camp sits about a quarter mile north of it. From the junction take the primitive, unmaintained Pyramid Creek Trail west and climb about 1,000 ft over a mile to a mile and a half into the upper basin between Emerald and Saska, around 7,100 ft. The tread is intermittent. Pushing to that camp rather than stopping at the junction costs an extra hour on the approach day and returns about the same on summit day. This is reported as the easiest and shortest of the Saska / Emerald / Cardinal trio's summit scrambles.
wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.season: Mid-Jul-Sep once the col and summit gullies clear. October adds larch colour and early-snow risk; before mid-July carry an axe for lingering snow and ice
hazards: Heavy blowdown and washouts on the lower North Fork Entiat Trail from past fires and storms; hot, shadeless valley bottom
Primitive upper Pyramid Creek trail leads to the high basin camp

wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.baseFinding:
The base is the col and the direction off it is west. From the basin camp, about 600 ft of gain on talus, scree or lingering snow reaches the Emerald-Saska Col at roughly 7,700 ft — a notch on the south ridge with a peak on either side. From the col, head west toward Saska. Emerald is the other way. If you leave the col climbing east you are on the neighbouring peak's ground.

The positive test is that you do not stay on the crest. The connecting ridge is narrow and knife-edged in places with steep drop-offs on both sides, so the usual line drops slightly onto its west flank to pick up an obvious scree-and-rock gully, then follows a cairned rising traverse back toward the crest. West flank, gully, cairned rising traverse. A party grimly balancing along the crest itself has missed the line rather than found the hard way.

The finish is counted in feet, not features: roughly 300 ft of final Class 3 on loose blocks gains the top. Test every hold — nothing here is fixed and no rope is standard, although the last exposed moves are steep enough that some parties carry a short handline for them.

The descent marker is a warning with a documented consequence: cliff bands sit below the south-west face. Stay well clear of them when the ground is snow-covered or icy. A winter party misjudging that descent line in icy conditions lost a ski over those cliffs. In early-to-mid season the continuous snow below the col gives a glissade or boot-ski; by August and September the same ground is loose scree and dirt that has to be walked slowly.

Loose rock is the theme of the whole cirque. Helmet, and do not stack the party directly above one another, from the moment you leave the basin.

wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.name: Lake Chelan: Lucerne and Emerald Park to Milham Pass

bivy.name: The basin between Emerald and Saska, and Milham Pass
bivy.notes: The high camp for the crest traverse, about a mile and a half beyond Fox Camp on the Pyramid trail, in the basin that separates Emerald Peak from Saska Peak. This is where a party stages to link Cardinal, Emerald, Saska and Pinnacle Mountain in a single push over Milham Pass at about 6,663 ft, which is the classic way to do these four and much the most efficient. From the basin you climb to the upper shelf just below the ridge between Emerald and Saska and pick up the broad gully to the summit. Cardinal is the highest of the group and the furthest, and it is the one that turns a two-day plan into three. The setting is superb and the ground is loose — expect scree and blocky scrambling rather than clean rock, and expect the descents to take longer than the ascents. Season is short at this height in a heavy year, realistically mid-July to early October, and the reason to come late is the larch and the reason not to is the water. Weigh that honestly: an August party that finds the tarns dry has a long, hot walk back down to fix it. Weather moves in from the west with little warning here and the basin is fully exposed.
bivy.water: Snowmelt tarns and rivulets in the basin, and these are the crux of the whole plan. They are dependable in early and mid summer, unreliable by mid-August, and in a dry year they are gone entirely by late August, at which point the nearest certain water is back down at Fox Camp. Do not commit to a high camp here in late season without either confirming water or carrying it up. Milham Pass itself has none.
bivy.permit: Glacier Peak Wilderness, free self-issue, party limit of twelve. Camp on durable ground and well back from the tarns. No campfires — forest-wide restrictions aside, there is no fuel at this elevation and the ground is fragile. The approach trails, including the Emerald Park, Domke Lake, North Fork Entiat and Pyramid Creek trails, have been closed under the Little Giant Fire closure; check its status with the Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest before you go.
bivy.capacity: A small number of tent-sized spots on benches and moraine in the upper basin; two or three parties at most, and less if you want flat ground

wa_saska_peak_emerald_saska_col.notes: Take the boat up Lake Chelan to Lucerne, then climb the trail past the Domke Lake junction and up Emerald Park Creek to Emerald Park, about 6.5 miles, and on another two miles to Milham Pass. Drop from the pass into the basin between Emerald and Saska and pick up the south-slopes route there. A long, remote approach that suits parties already on the Lake Chelan side.
hazards: Boat access up Lake Chelan, then a long, remote approach of about 6.5 miles to Emerald Park and two more to Milham Pass
Drop from the pass into the basin between Emerald and Saska; route-finding needed
Loose rock and rockfall in the Emerald-Saska col basin and along the summit ridge; helmet advised
Lingering snow and ice in the col and summit gullies into early-to-mid July
Cliff bands below the south-west face have caught descending parties in icy or snowy conditions
Narrow, sometimes knife-edged connecting crest to be avoided rather than followed

wa_silver_star_ne_ridge.name: SR-20 pullout, Burgundy Creek climbers' trail, the Bench, Burgundy Col
camps: Burgundy Creek bench camp — west side
Burgundy Col high camp — west side, the Wine Spires
Upper scree benches below Burgundy Col — west side
wa_silver_star_ne_ridge.notes:
Park at the broad pullout and overlook on SR-20 near milepost 165-166, about four miles east of Washington Pass, where a sign points toward Silver Star Mountain.

Drop down the embankment roughly 150 to 200 ft to Early Winters Creek and cross on a log. Logjams shift year to year, so scout up and down for the best crossing and be prepared to ford in high water or early season when the creek runs cold and fast with snowmelt. Treat this crossing as your last reliable water until camp.

On the far bank pick up the unofficial but well-defined climbers' trail that climbs the timbered rib on the west (left) side of the Burgundy Creek drainage. From there it climbs relentlessly and steeply through forest and brush for roughly 2,500-3,000 ft with almost no switchbacks and only fleeting water access early on. The tread erodes and is easy to lose in the timber.
hazards: Early Winters Creek crossing: log can be wet or washed out; ford in high water
Steep eroding brushy tread easy to lose in the timber; no water between creek and bench
Loose microwave-sized blocks in the gully above the bench
Loose kitty-litter slabs on the final traverse into Burgundy Col
Loose alpine rock on the summit
wa_silver_star_ne_ridge.baseFinding:
The unmistakable break on this approach is the bench, at roughly 6,400-6,700 ft: the grade suddenly eases onto an open larch-and-heather shelf with several established campsites and usually a seasonal trickle or snowmelt nearby. That is the standard overnight camp and the natural turnaround check for a day trip.

Above the bench there is a gully running obviously and directly to Burgundy Col. That gully is the wrong one — it is loose and exposed. Instead stay left and follow the trail up the gully directly above camp. Within it, stay climber's left of the gully proper: the bed holds loose microwave-sized blocks, while the left side is unpleasant kitty-litter-covered slab but far less dangerous. Near the head of the gully make an ascending traverse to the right, under the cliffs, over heather-covered slabs into the col at roughly 7,800 ft. This gully and traverse is where parties describe the real crux of route-finding, both up and down. The col — not the glacier — is where the route proper begins; from there trend toward the northeast side of the west summit.

wa_silver_star_ne_ridge.name: Silver Star Creek from the north

bivy.name: Lone Fir Campground, SR 20
bivy.notes: A roadside vehicle campground rather than a site on any approach — it is for sleeping the night before, not for the climb. It opens around May and closes with the first serious snow, tracking the same window as everything else here. The whole area is gated by the SR 20 winter closure, which shuts in late November or early December and reopens in spring, with the date driven by avalanche work and storm damage rather than the calendar. In closed months the pullout is inside the gated section and the approach becomes a long ski or snowmobile trip.
bivy.water: No drinking water at the campground. Early Winters Creek runs alongside and needs filtering; Klipchuck and Early Winters campgrounds, farther east, have drinking water in season.
bivy.permit: Per-night campground fee; no wilderness permit involved. The unmarked Silver Star Creek pullout that starts the west approach is not itself a signed fee site — check current signage rather than assuming either way.
bivy.capacity: 27 developed first-come, first-served sites for tents and small vehicles

wa_silver_star_ne_ridge.notes: Park where SR-20 crosses Silver Star Creek and follow the trail up the east side of the creek for about two miles. Where it fades near 4,850 ft, trend west across the valley and climb open talus toward Burgundy Spire and onto the glacier. Best on continuous spring snow, when it makes a good ski or snowshoe approach; once the valley melts out it turns brushy and swampy and Burgundy Col is the better choice.
hazards: Valley turns brushy and swampy once the snow melts out; best on continuous spring snow
Tread fades near 4,850 ft; cross the valley and climb open talus toward Burgundy Spire
Crevasses on the Silver Star Glacier approach
Loose alpine rock on the summit

wa_southeast_ridge_se_corner.name: Shannon Ridge and the Sulphide Glacier to the notch on the southeast ridge
wa_southeast_ridge_se_corner.notes:
From the Shannon Ridge Trailhead, climb east-northeast up Shannon Ridge and onto the Sulphide Glacier — the standard Shuksan approach, and the same one the Sulphide Glacier route uses. Most parties camp on the large flat plateau around 6,400 ft, which is the usual staging point for summit day.

The snow between roughly 5,400 and 6,400 ft is where visibility bites: it is featureless open ground and parties report it as the tricky stretch in reduced visibility. Above camp the upper Sulphide is mellow, with a few small crevasses that are generally stepped over.

This route then leaves the standard finish. Where the Sulphide Glacier route walks to the foot of the summit pyramid and takes its Class 3-4 gully, this one gains the ridge at a notch further east and climbs about six pitches of well-featured 5.3 rock to the top.
wa_southeast_ridge_se_corner.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, once the Sulphide is walkable and the rock is out from under snow
hazards: Featureless snow between 5,400 and 6,400 ft is genuinely hard to navigate in reduced visibility
Crevasses on the Sulphide Glacier, small but present, increasingly open late season
Active rockfall near the bootpack around 5,400 ft, worse in the afternoon; go early
Bergschrund crossing on the upper Sulphide that gets trickier as the glacier opens
Limited protection on sparsely protectable 5.3 rock; severe exposure on both sides of the crest
Descent rappels a gully shared with the standard route; parties above are a rockfall source
Blue ice August-September; sun-softened snow bridges in the afternoon
wa_southeast_ridge_se_corner.baseFinding:
The notch is the route, and you can feel it rather than see it. Gaining the southeast ridge happens at a prominent notch at the top of the upper Sulphide. In cloud, work up the glacier until the snow stops rising and you can step onto rock at a low point in the ridgeline with ground falling away on the far side. A notch you can stand in with air behind you is the arrival; a rock wall in front of you with snow still under your feet is not.

The discriminator against the standard route, and it is the mistake to avoid: the Sulphide Glacier route's finish is a fourth-class gully up the summit pyramid, and it is the line almost everyone on the mountain is walking toward. If you find yourself queueing at the bottom of a gully with a bootpack into it, you are at the standard finish, not at this route's start. This route gains a ridge crest, not a gully.

Second test, on the rope: the climbing here is six pitches of extremely well-featured rock that parties describe as easy in boots, with limited protection and severe exposure on both sides of the crest. If your first pitch is a gully with walls either side of you rather than a crest with air either side of you, you have started in the wrong place. Exposure on both sides is the confirmation.

What walking past it looks like: continuing up the Sulphide beyond the notch brings you under the summit pyramid's south side, where the standard gully is. That is the descent for this route — the same gully is rappelled on the way down — so recognising it does not mean you are lost, but it does mean you have gone past the start.

wa_southeast_ridge_se_corner.name: Lake Ann and the Fisher Chimneys to the summit pyramid
wa_southeast_ridge_se_corner.notes:
From the Lake Ann Trailhead on SR 542, follow the whole Fisher Chimneys route to the foot of the summit pyramid: Lake Ann Trail #600 to the saddle, the climbers' path east to the chimneys, about 1,000 ft of class 3–4 scrambling through them, Winnie's Slide onto the Upper Curtis Glacier, then Hell's Highway onto the upper Sulphide Glacier.

Longer, steeper and more technical than the Shannon Ridge approach, and most parties take two or three days, camping at Lake Ann or above the chimneys. Where the Fisher Chimneys route finishes up the central gully, this one trends right off the glacier and takes the southeast ridge instead.
hazards: Rockfall inside the Fisher Chimneys (about 1,000 ft of class 3-4), especially with parties above
Steep snow or ice on Winnie's Slide, firm before the sun reaches it
Crevasses on the Upper Curtis Glacier
Hell's Highway crosses exposed slopes below the Upper Curtis icefall
Limited protection on sparsely protectable 5.3 rock; severe exposure on both sides of the crest
Descent rappels a gully shared with the standard route; parties above are a rockfall source
wa_southeast_ridge_se_corner.baseFinding: You arrive on the upper Sulphide from Hell's Highway, so the summit pyramid is ahead of you and the southeast ridge is its right-hand skyline. Do not head for the central gully, the line with the fixed rappel anchors, which is the standard finish. Work right across the top of the glacier to the notch where the ridge meets the snow. This is the same arrival the Shannon Ridge approach makes.

wa_sw_ridge.name: Agnes Creek from High Bridge, into the Blue Glacier basin
camps: High camp above the Blue Glacier
wa_sw_ridge.notes: From High Bridge, follow the Pacific Crest Trail and the Agnes Creek trail about nine to ten miles, cross Agnes Creek on a log and bushwhack steeply into the upper Blue basin, gaining about 5,000 ft. Camp on the exposed rock ridge above the Blue Glacier, directly below the east side of the Gunsight peaks.
hazards: Steep off-trail bushwhack of about 5,000 ft into the upper Blue basin after a log crossing of Agnes Creek
Crevassed glacier travel to reach the high camp below the peaks
Loose blocky climbing on the opening pitches
Exposure on the summit ridge crest
Dirty, loose, cold moat at the base of the notch after the descent rappels
Remote multi-day setting with self-rescue only

wa_sw_ridge.name: Downey Creek and the Chickamin Glacier
wa_sw_ridge.notes: From the Downey Creek trailhead on the Suiattle River Road at about 1,400 ft, follow the Downey Creek and Bachelor Creek trails to Bachelor Meadows and Cub Pass, then go past Cub Lake, over Itswoot Pass and across the Dome Glacier to the Chickamin-Dome col. From the col, descend onto the heavily crevassed Chickamin Glacier and traverse it to the west side of the Gunsight peaks. This is a long, fully glaciated approach with a rope, crevasse gear and route-finding needed throughout.
hazards: Heavily crevassed Chickamin Glacier traverse; rope and crevasse gear needed
Dome Glacier crossing to the Chickamin-Dome col
Fully glaciated approach with route-finding needed throughout
Loose blocky climbing on the opening pitches
Exposure on the summit ridge crest
Remote multi-day setting with self-rescue only

wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.name: Over the pass at the head of the river road, then east and down to the lake
wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.notes:
From the trailhead at the end of the river road, climb to the pass at about 5,392 ft - or to the nearby col used as an alternative when the pass is corniced - and then travel east, descending and traversing through the basin beyond, to the lake at about 4,170 ft, which sits just north-east of the peak. From the lake you boot or skin directly to the foot of the route, changing to crampons or ascent plates as the snow firms up higher.

This is the approach that suits the route's season: the couloir is a snow line, so the party wants it early, which is also when the pass is a straightforward snow climb rather than a scramble.
wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.season: Spring into early summer, while the couloir still holds continuous snow
hazards: a corniced pass early in the season, with an alternative col that carries its own hazards
a descent east from the pass that must be re-climbed at the end of the day
avalanche terrain in the couloir and the basin below it in spring
wet-snow release and rockfall out of the couloir once the sun reaches the face
a remote basin with a long retreat and no trail on the eastern side
wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.baseFinding:
The couloir is visible from the lake and that is the point of approaching from this side. From the water, look south-west at the peak: the route is the obvious north-facing snow line that splits the summit block itself. Pick it out before you start moving, because from underneath the flanking gullies all look alike.

The positive test is where the line ends. It must top out on the summit block, not on the ridge beside it. A couloir that finishes at a notch with more mountain above it and to one side is one of the flanking gullies and not the route.

The second test is aspect. This is the north side: it should be the shaded flank, holding firmer snow than anything around it in the morning and going soft late. If the snow you are standing on is in early sun, you have come round onto an eastern or western flank.

The third test is continuity. The route is a single continuous line from the basin to the top of the block. If the snow you are following breaks into disconnected patches with rock steps between them, you are either too late in the season for it or on a different feature.

And check the mountain. There is a similarly named peak elsewhere in the range that is reached from an entirely different valley and has nothing to do with this one. The confirmation here is that the lake lies immediately north-east of your peak and the summit stands directly across it from you.

wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.name: From the valley on the east, reaching the lake basin from below
wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.notes:
The lake basin can also be reached from the valley to the east, which is entered by boat or floatplane and then by road and trail up the valley floor. This is the approach the other route on this peak uses, and it puts a party at the lake without any pass to cross.

Treat the detail of it with caution. The published descriptions of this peak disagree about which drainage is followed off the valley trail and how far the lake is from the road, and the two accounts cannot both be right - so plan this variant from current maps and imagery rather than from a written description, and expect the off-trail section to be unmarked and steep.
wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.season: Summer, once the valley trail is open and the basin is snow-free enough to walk
hazards: an approach that depends on boat or floatplane schedules to reach the valley at all
an unmarked, steep off-trail push into the basin with no tread to follow out
conflicting written descriptions of which drainage is used, so navigate from maps rather than prose
avalanche terrain in the couloir in spring
a long committing distance from any road
wa_trapper_mountain_north_couloir.baseFinding:
The fixed point on this side is the lake, and everything above it is read off the peak itself. The lake sits immediately north-east of the summit, so from the water the mountain stands to the south-west and the route faces you.

The route is the continuous north-facing snow line cleaving the summit block. It must finish on the block. A gully that tops out on the ridge to either side of the summit is a flanking line, not the route.

Use shade as the confirmation: the north side holds shadow while the basin around it is lit, and the snow in it stays firm longest in the morning.

Because the approach from this side is unmarked, fix your line into the basin on the way in. There is no tread to follow back out, and the basin has no obvious exit when seen from above.
